files.text:
# Exploratory CPU final readouts

This experiment asks whether skipping unused final-block query, output and MLP
rows improves the already confirmed retained-prefix CPU scorer. Production code,
loader defaults and server behavior remain unchanged. The temporary scorer is
owned by `benchmarks/analysis/torch/readout/scorer.py`; it is removed or replaced
only after a separately reviewed experiment establishes a useful boundary.

One FP32 CPU Kai base owns the weights. Retained and selected resources build
independent eager snapshots of the same exact 25-token prefix. Each call encodes
complete original requests, admits the entire batch before removing the prefix,
and forks fresh stock caches. Mixed, mismatched or prefix-overlapping readouts
fall back through the original production tensor owner without encoding again.
The existing fixed weights/config/device/encoder lifetime, no backbone hooks,
disabled CPU autocast, default RoPE and stock SDPA requirements still apply.

The selected path captures absolute suffix positions, full early causal mask and
full suffix RoPE before any cache update. It executes the first 27 stock blocks.
The last block retains every suffix K/V row and the complete prefix K/V, while
query/output/MLP/final normalization operate on six candidate rows and one query
row. Ordered duplicates and padded candidate slots are preserved. Its explicit
mask permits each key only at or before the readout's original absolute position.
This real-arithmetic equivalence does not establish identical FP32 rounding or
native kernel dispatch.

## Fixed screen

After independent tiny block/core tests and source review, the owned launcher is:

```sh
python -m benchmarks.analysis.torch.readout.run .models/Decision-2.0-Kai-0.6B \
  --output benchmarks/analysis/results/torch-readout-first8.json
```

One worker has a 180-second cap. The runner admits the original ordered 77 inputs,
all nine original model asset hashes, dataset/reference identities and archived
historical confirmations before selecting the canonical first eight. B8, FP32,
eight intraop threads, max length 512 and zero token cache are fixed. Attention,
precision and native HF eligibility flags are observed without modification.
The original thread count is restored before successful completion is saved.

O is ordinary production scoring, R final production retained-prefix scoring,
and S selected final readouts. Warm O/R/S, then ordinary O/R/S/S/R/O, then separate
intrusive R/S profiles: 11 cohorts, 88 outcomes. Every output must preserve exact
IDs, gold labels, complete ranks, selections and accuracy, with original logit
absolute/relative tolerance 1e-3 and probability absolute tolerance 1e-4. All
ordinary arms are also compared pairwise. No tolerance changes are permitted.
Each raw cohort is persisted first, then checked against the reference and
available arm anchors. The first drift, rank, failure or timing violation stops
further calls, preserving partial history and the pending cohort list.

Ordinary timing is the existing complete-cohort metric, including encoding,
packing, fresh cache construction, model execution and host decision output.
Setup, source hashes, journal serialization and profiler reduction are outside
that metric. Two observations per arm are exploratory, with no speed gate.
`accepted` and `performance_passed` remain false even when quality/dispatch pass.

The separate native profiles must observe 28 full-query CPU flash calls for R
and 27 full-query plus one seven-query call for S, retaining eight K/V heads and
all 192 key/value rows. The selected mask has shape [8,1,7,192]. Eligibility flags
alone do not prove this dispatch; missing/incompatible evidence fails the gate.
Profiles are intrusive and their grouped operator times do not establish the
last layer's share of ordinary latency.

Every completed raw cohort is journaled before validation. Invalid clock values
retain null plus their original representation; partial profiler failures retain
produced predictions, and unexecuted cohorts remain pending.
The journal has one immutable raw entry per produced cohort. Main rows add
reference and anchor reports afterward; their original raw fields must agree.
Main/journal/source archive paths are exclusive. Current runtime, benchmark,
tests, docs and relevant
installed dependency source are frozen and checked outside each body and at the
end. Historical identities come from executed archives, independently of later
legitimate production changes. These observations do not attest every native
binary/imported object. All raw receipts and failed attempts remain immutable.

Extended K/V retention remains unchanged; this is not a memory ceiling. A useful
first-eight result would require a separately declared full77 R-relative B8/B1
confirmation with the original four speed gates before any production proposal.
No held-out quality, online/server capacity, GPU or 20x claim follows from this
screen. Under assumed uniform layer costs, eliminating an entire last block
would illustrate 28/27 speedup; no CPU profile establishes that uniformity, and
this candidate still computes full K/V.

files.text:
# Scalar confirmation of selected CPU readouts

The independently audited first-eight screen preserved all 88 outcomes and
native CPU flash geometry. Its two retained/selected ordinary ratios were
1.0245579 and 1.0090246: descriptive median 1.0167913, below the original 1.02
promotion threshold. Two samples and intrusive profiles neither establish a
full-cohort benefit nor decisively reject it. Their immutable source archive and
raw audit identify that execution independently of later source inventories.

The next assay is scalar first, using `benchmarks/analysis/torch/readout/confirm.py`.
Production, original scorer/core and first-eight driver/docs remain unchanged.
One shared FP32 CPU base supplies independent eager retained and selected prefix
resources, with fresh stock caches inside each call. The authoritative original
ordered 77 requests, six-candidate menus, reference token vectors, model identity
and all nine asset hashes remain fixed. Prefix length25, max length512, zero token
cache and eight intraop threads are retained. Attention/precision policies and
HF eligibility flags are observed without modification.

```sh
python -m benchmarks.analysis.torch.readout.confirm .models/Decision-2.0-Kai-0.6B \
  --output benchmarks/analysis/results/torch-readout-confirm-b1.json
```

One owned worker has a fresh 180-second cap. Screen retained/selected, warm
retained/selected, then five paired measurements in AB, BA, AB, BA, AB order:
14 cohorts, 1,078 outcomes. Every produced raw cohort is saved to the exclusive
journal and main receipt before validation. Main rows then add reference and
available-arm-anchor comparisons; raw journal fields remain identical. Stop
subsequent cohorts after the first source/policy/admission, numerical/rank/failure,
accuracy or timing violation, retaining outputs, error and pending cohorts.
The existing runner attempts the complete scalar cohort before returning its
raw outcomes; failed cases remain in that cohort's denominator. This protocol
does not add validation inside the measured per-case loop.
Nonfinite clock values retain null plus their original representation.

Quality retains exact IDs/gold labels, full ranks, choices and accuracy, logit
absolute/relative tolerance1e-3 and probability absolute tolerance1e-4. Measured
arms are compared pairwise as well as against the original FP32 reference.
Timing is the existing complete-cohort metric, including original encoding,
packing, fresh cache construction, model execution and host decision results;
setup, source checks and journal writes are outside it. There are no profiles or
RSS samplers inside measured calls. Prior first-eight B8 dispatch remains prior
representative evidence; current scalar timed dispatch is unobserved.

All four original performance conditions must pass relative to retained prefix:
paired median at least1.02, interpolated sample p05 greater than1, aggregate
baseline/candidate cohort-time ratio greater than1 and candidate cohort p95 no
greater than baseline p95. Sample p05 is not a confidence bound. A speed-only
negative retains `completed=True`, `quality_passed=True`, `performance_passed=False`
and `accepted=False`, and the worker exits zero for a complete quality assay.
All five pairs are measured before deciding performance; slow samples are kept.

Current runtime/benchmark/dependency source, tests and this protocol are frozen
and checked outside every body and at completion. Old captures are admitted from
their executed archived text/hash inventories, never current dynamic file globs
or later documentation bytes. Current source equality is checked separately.
Asset hashes are streamed before loading and after the assay; native binary and
imported object identity are not independently attested. Original thread settings
must be restored before any successful completion is saved. All raw receipts,
failed attempts, source archives and owned worker terminal evidence are preserved.

If scalar fails any performance condition, stop; no B8 model job follows. If
scalar passes and its raw evidence is independently audited, a separately
declared fresh B8 full77 assay must pass the same conditions before any production
proposal. This scalar-only launcher cannot start B8. No production change,
held-out quality, memory ceiling, server/online capacity, GPU or 20x claim follows.

## Observed scalar result

The full scalar assay completed all 14 cohorts and 1,078 outcomes. The independent
standard-library audit reconstructed the original numerical gates, all complete
ranks and selections, and all five paired timing metrics. Every cohort retains
67/77 correct decisions, with no failed or missing outcome. Maximum reference
logit/probability drift is 9.954e-6/1.560e-6, within the unchanged gates.

| Original performance condition | Observed | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Paired median at least 1.02 | 1.00853x | Fail |
| Sample p05 greater than 1 | 0.98916x | Fail |
| Aggregate cohort-time ratio greater than 1 | 1.00678x | Pass |
| Candidate/baseline cohort p95 at most 1 | 0.99869 | Pass |

The five retained/selected ratios are 1.01438, **0.99881**, **0.98675**, 1.00853
and 1.02606. These samples do not establish a confidence bound or a consistent
speed improvement. Reject this candidate under the declared scalar selection
policy; no B8 confirmation follows. Production remains the retained-prefix path
with its complete final block. The assay remains `completed=True` and
`quality_passed=True`, with `performance_passed=False` and `accepted=False`.

The owned inference worker exited zero and was reaped in 131.730 seconds under
its 180-second cap. Threads were restored before completion. Each resource
retained 5,734,400 logical prefix bytes; setup took 83.683 ms for retained and
74.516 ms for selected. These are separate setup observations, not peak-memory
or amortized speed claims. Scalar dispatch was unprofiled; native dispatch
evidence remains scoped to the prior first-eight B8 captures.

The [raw audit](../../../../benchmarks/analysis/results/torch-readout-confirm-b1-review.json)
and [owned audit execution](../../../../benchmarks/analysis/results/torch-readout-confirm-b1-review.execution.json)
retain the exact producer, arguments, raw pins, terminal status and its
0.798-second execution under a 60-second cap. The executed 65-source archive
SHA256 is `8cd255f6f91ab64d88b744a9f2856f78c1a8ce538c2acf94c4916931d6616503`.
That immutable archive contains the prospective protocol; this result section
was appended after the audit. Later historical admission must identify the run
from archived bytes rather than require this updated document to match them.

# CUDA numerical admission

Prospective declaration, 2026-10-05. The Wyat engine task owns this bounded
experiment. Production CUDA precision and default loading remain unchanged.
The earlier [feasibility audit](cuda.md) distinguishes the released BF16 CUDA
recipe from a strict FP32 control.

Fresh read-only observations found the RTX 4070 Ti at zero utilization, about
128–131 MiB allocated, and no compute-process rows. These observations are not
a reservation. Require an uncontended pre-allocation observation and reject
foreign compute ownership before each batch and after the cohort. Do not signal
or alter other jobs.
Retain contention, unsupported settings, allocation errors and timeouts.

The private experiment directory uses an existing read-only Torch
`2.12.1+cu130` installation, Python 3.12 and a separate Transformers `5.18.0`
dependency layer. Existing environments are unchanged; no Torch download is
needed. Record full package/build identities and exact source bytes, including
the maintained Qwen and SDPA integration. The nine canonical files, including
attribution, total about 1.519 GB; their bytes, dataset and CPU reference
must match the manifest before device allocation. No arbitrary remote code is
loaded. The model identity remains `kai:1f5525e01de43a724c71824579ef5195595fba916ce1e02be7bbbbea50f25cee`.

The first arm is one complete batch-one cohort of all 77 original BANKING77
training-source six-choice cases. Load through the CPU FP32 path, validate all
token IDs/endpoints/query positions against the frozen CPU reference, then move
all floating parameters and buffers to CUDA FP32. Preserve encoder, candidate
order, endpoint gathering, causal padding and the FP32 head. Use modern IEEE
global and CUDA matmul settings, disabled autocast and forced SDPA MATH.
Do not call production CUDA `score_many` for this control because it explicitly
enables BF16 autocast. Verify observed projection/head dtypes and autocast state;
recording those fields without enforcing the declared precision is insufficient.

Use the unchanged full-ranking and selected-choice gates, logit absolute/relative
tolerance `1e-3`, probability tolerance `1e-4`, no failures and no accuracy drop
against the frozen CPU reference. The original dataset/reference/input hashes
are respectively `0020d9a3…`, `b8a90b31…` and `fd5dd942…`. Retain every output or
failure in the denominator. A canonical runner that has not returned its entire
cohort after a timeout supplies no completed partial-quality claim.

Only a reviewed, immutable successful FP32 batch-one receipt permits either a
batch-eight FP32 control or a separate ordinary released-CUDA arm. Keep identities
and gates fixed. Batch-eight additionally requires the declared memory margin.
Released CUDA uses its existing lossless BF16 Linear storage and BF16 backbone
autocast, with FP32 residuals, norms and head. A failed strict gate rejects that
arm; the upstream recipe does not waive numerical admission.

Run each arm in one owned fresh worker with a 180-second whole-process cap and
process-group cleanup. Restore precision state, remove observers and preserve
late-write/cleanup failures so completed-quality flags cannot survive a failed
required boundary. Store raw receipts and exact source archives; independently
review the actual result before using it as a downstream control.

This is numerical feasibility, not a latency benchmark or production promotion.
Observer hooks and a single cold cohort cannot support a speed comparison.
Checkpoint exposure is unknown; these are 77 unique training-source development
examples, not held-out Wyat quality. Repetitions would not add independent labels.

# CUDA feasibility and precision contract

Inspected on 2026-10-05. This is a read-only contract audit, not a CUDA
benchmark. No weights were transferred, no model was loaded remotely, and no
GPU workload was launched. The existing CPU FP32 reference remains the quality
denominator.

## Observed local execution policy

[`torch.py`](../../wyat/backends/kai/torch.py) loads the backbone into FP32,
validates its weights, and accepts CPU or CUDA devices. CUDA requires reported
BF16 support. Before moving to CUDA, only Linear weights/biases whose BF16
round-trip is exact are stored in BF16. Every CUDA `score_many` call then
enables BF16 autocast for the backbone. Embeddings, norms, residuals and head
weights remain FP32; the candidate head explicitly disables autocast and casts
its inputs to FP32. Tokens, endpoint positions, causal ordering, choice-only
semantics and host response computation are shared with CPU.

This matches the inspected released Kai GPU precision recipe, rather than an
all-FP32 CUDA policy. Source is pinned to
[`decision2/qwen.py` at cd49ea3](https://huggingface.co/vllm-sr/Decision-2.0-Kai-0.6B/blob/cd49ea3813fd8ba0928a9a23ef6c9a0f2f0cd764/decision2/qwen.py),
SHA-256 `62df8de050d38cd92dc68c12de7d9b65d041a14317feda02ff8ddafc3c69c779`.
Its local retained bytes were inspected; the browser could not reopen that
file in this audit. The pinned
[`decision2/fast.py`](https://huggingface.co/vllm-sr/Decision-2.0-Kai-0.6B/blob/cd49ea3813fd8ba0928a9a23ef6c9a0f2f0cd764/decision2/fast.py)
requires HIP and Transformers 5.17 for installation, with fused kernels further
limited to gfx942. Those optimizations do not establish an NVIDIA fast path.

Exact weight storage is not exact activation arithmetic. BF16 autocast rounds
eligible operations even when parameters are FP32. An outer disabled-autocast
context does not override the enabled context inside `score_many`.
[PyTorch AMP documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/amp.html)
describes these nested regions and operation-specific dtypes. FP32 head tensors
also do not prevent process-global TF32 matmul policy from affecting head
Linear operations. The adapter does not configure that policy. PyTorch 2.14
provides IEEE precision settings and warns against mixing them with legacy
`allow_tf32` controls.
[CUDA precision documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/notes/cuda.html)

SDPA backend selection can change rounding. The math implementation supports
FP32, while fused kernels have their own eligibility restrictions and numerical
behavior. Record dispatch rather than equating `sdpa` with FlashAttention.
[SDPA documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html)

## Observed resource boundary and unknowns

Root's fresh read-only probe reported an RTX 4070 Ti, 12,282 MiB total memory,
6,364 MiB used and 98% utilization. The established concurrent training workload
is outside this experiment. Apparent free memory is not permission or evidence
of idle compute. No CUDA inference experiment should contend with it.

Remote PyTorch/Transformers versions, CUDA build, precision settings, actual
BF16 capability check, attention dispatch, workspace peaks and Wyat numerical
parity are unknown. Local CPU fixture tests establish encoding/head mechanics;
the released-weight CPU/MLX assay does not test CUDA. No current evidence
supports or falsifies CUDA passing the strict FP32 quality gates.

## Smallest useful experiment after an idle window

Use an experiment-only forward with the production encoder, backbone, head and
endpoint gather. Load through the CPU path, move **all** floating weights to
CUDA FP32, and execute with CUDA autocast disabled. Do not call the existing
CUDA `score_many` for this control, because it re-enables BF16. Do not change
production dtype policy merely to create the control.

In a separate process, record installed versions/builds and save/restore the
version-appropriate precision settings. For PyTorch 2.14, request IEEE global
and CUDA matmul precision without mixing legacy flags. Force
`sdpa_kernel(SDPBackend.MATH)` for the initial control and verify parameter,
head-input and projection dtypes in an untimed diagnostic. This controls the
main reduced-precision choices; it does not prove CPU/GPU bitwise identity.
PyTorch explicitly permits different results across devices and batched forms.
[Numerical accuracy documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/notes/numerical_accuracy.html)

Freeze source bytes, artifact identity and the full 77-case input/reference
receipt before loading. Start with batch one and maximum length 512; retain
every output or failure. Gate every selected candidate and full ranking, logits
at absolute/relative tolerance 1e-3, and probabilities at 1e-4. Then check the
same cohort at batch eight if measured memory permits. Any drift, missing row,
unsupported setting or allocation failure remains a failure/unknown, not an
omitted sample.

Only after the FP32 control passes, compare the ordinary CUDA BF16 policy to
the same frozen reference and separately to the FP32 CUDA control. A failed
BF16 gate rejects that candidate under the current quality contract; matching
upstream's dtype recipe does not waive the gate. Keep shape/backend changes as
separate arms. Run one warmup and three measured repetitions per arm, with a
600-second whole-process cap and early exit after a material quality failure.

Include encoding, transfers and host response in complete-request latency.
Synchronize around any separately reported device interval; GPU submission
alone is not completion time. Capture allocated/reserved/peak CUDA memory and
own-process diagnostics outside the timed region, and require uncontended
occupancy observations before and after. Performance under a busy training
job cannot establish a standalone speedup. This proposal is prepared, not run.

# Packed gate/up storage feasibility

Hypothesis: one packed gate/up backing can serve both the separate-projection
control and combined-projection candidate without retaining duplicate weights.
This addresses the measured CUDA gate/up target, about 29.0% and 27.2% of
representative kernel-duration sums at batches one and eight. Those fractions
are diagnostic; they do not establish a complete-inference Amdahl bound.

A private CPU probe used the actual Kai layer-zero BF16 gate/up/down weights
restored to FP32, and the retained first-eight activation of shape 1536×1024.
The cached activation and its capture declaration were hash-pinned; consumed
model tensor payload identities were recorded before loading. Original Qwen MLP,
storage-only control and packed candidate output hashes were identical, with
finite maximum absolute error zero. Nine tests passed, including twenty tiny
Hypothesis examples and rejected owner states. Tiny random cases test mechanics,
not the deployment distribution.

The control's two contiguous row views and candidate's combined parameter share
one **25,165,824-byte (24 MiB)** backing. Counting all three parameter tensors
would double-count that storage. Replaced parameter wrappers expired; this does
not measure allocator/RSS release or prove absence of arbitrary external aliases.
The probe assumes a fresh, unhooked, gradient-disabled evaluation owner with no
optimizer, checkpoint writes or external parameter-identity contract.

This supports local CPU mechanics and one real layer's outputs. It supplies no
whole-model decision, CUDA parity, latency, speedup, memory-reservation or
production claim. An initial pytest collection failed on an unrelated protected
temporary-directory sibling before tests ran. The retry used byte-identical
source in a task-owned directory; both outcomes remain retained.

The next candidate needs explicit device/storage ownership. Independently
moving control and candidate modules to CUDA can copy their aliased views into
separate allocations. Moving the complete owned model first, packing one layer
on-device, and recreating both control views is a narrow candidate; retained and
peak allocation/reservation remain measurements. CPU storage proof does not
establish CUDA alias preservation. Storage-only control must independently pass
the existing CPU/CUDA references before comparing complete packed inference.
All77 logits, probabilities, selections, full rankings, failures and labeled
accuracy remain gated; promotion needs warmed paired whole-body measurements
and resource/lifecycle challenges. No such CUDA experiment has been released.

Evidence: [real-layer receipt](../../../benchmarks/analysis/results/cuda-packing-feasibility.json),
[provenance companion](../../../benchmarks/analysis/results/cuda-packing-provenance.json),
and [independent read-only review](../../../benchmarks/analysis/results/cuda-packing-local-review.json).
The exact executed source is retained as text, with both the successful owned wall
and initial collection-failure wall. The current full checkpoint SHA matches the
original pin; current per-key payloads match their pre-load recorded identities.
The local runtime is Torch 2.14.1, HF 5.18.0 and Python 3.12; this supplies no
numerical/device result for the remote Torch 2.12.1 runtime. The companion retains
unobserved historical environment/hash intervals as unknown rather than filling
them retroactively.

files.text:
# CUDA precision policy ownership

The exact Torch v2.12.1 tagged source supports **process-wide** ownership of
SDPA selection and FP32 precision. This replaces the earlier inference from
local Torch 2.14 source. The installed CUDA binary and a concurrent execution
race have not been independently inspected or exercised.

`globalContext()` owns one function-static `Context`. SDPA setters mutate its
ordinary fields; the FP32 getter resolves inherited settings before returning
an effective value. Python bindings invoke that owner.
[Context implementation](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/v2.12.1/aten/src/ATen/Context.cpp),
[fields](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/v2.12.1/aten/src/ATen/Context.h),
[Python bindings](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/v2.12.1/torch/csrc/Module.cpp).

The public SDPA context snapshots backends, changes global flags and restores
its snapshot in `finally`, without a lock or task-local owner. Consequently,
overlapping threads or an asynchronous yield inside a scope can affect another
inference or restore stale settings. This consequence is inferred from source;
it is not a measured race.
[Attention context](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/v2.12.1/torch/nn/attention/__init__.py).

Saving an effective precision getter and restoring it through a leaf setter can
turn an inherited setting into an explicit override. Effective read-back equality
does not establish restoration of the hidden inheritance tree. Existing serial
research workers own their process; cleanup claims retain this distinction.
[Precision properties](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/v2.12.1/torch/backends/__init__.py),
[inheritance implementation](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/v2.12.1/aten/src/ATen/Context.cpp).

The smallest coherent deployment candidate is one dedicated process with a
fixed precision/backend policy configured before admitting work. Incompatible
policies need separate processes. A per-application lock cannot control unrelated
Torch callers. This proposes an ownership boundary; it releases no serving
change. Numerical, causal, shape, cancellation and resource gates still apply.
IEEE matmul remains distinct from attention's internal arithmetic.
[Public controls](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.12/notes/cuda.html#tensorfloat-32-tf32-on-ampere-and-later-devices).

`cuda-policy-ownership-review.json` retains URLs, line references, observed and
inferred claims, and limits. Canonical source bytes/hashes were unavailable to
the web reader; hashes remain unknown. No GPU job, private payload transfer or
production edit accompanied this investigation.

files.text:
# CUDA FP32 efficient-attention results

The pinned Kai reference gains modest complete-body speed under the unchanged
numerical gates: median paired speedup **1.0565x at B1** and **1.0653x at B8**.
The comparison uses forced math attention versus the causal Boolean-mask
efficient-attention adapter, with FP32 weights, disabled autocast and IEEE
global/matmul settings. It is not a comparison against the released BF16 recipe,
an online server benchmark, a universal fastest-engine claim or a 20x result.

The [prospective protocol](latency.md) and five-file declaration
`a26d5be4…` remain unchanged. All four runs use the same 48-source archive
`21b3fa50…`, the original 44 assets, CPU reference, CUDA FP32 control and corrected
first-eight screens. All twenty production sources remain unchanged.

## Numerical confirmation

Each batch mode runs both ordinary arms over all 77 cases before profiling its
first batch. Independently reconstructed confirmations retain 156 outcomes at
B1 and 170 at B8. Both arms preserve every selected choice and full ranking,
with 67 correct of 77 and no failed or missing results. The candidate's maximum
CPU-reference logit/probability differences are `1.2517e-5 / 2.4516e-6` at B1
and `1.2875e-5 / 2.7318e-6` at B8, inside the original `1e-3` absolute/relative
logit and `1e-4` probability gates.

Representative candidate profiles each contain 28 public SDPA calls, 28 private
efficient calls, 28 forward calls and 28 actual FP32 SM80 CUTLASS attention
kernels, with no fallback. Math profiles contain 28 math calls and no efficient
attention kernels. Profiles remain intrusive diagnostics. FP32 tensors and
IEEE matmul settings do not establish the attention kernel's internal arithmetic.

## Warmed paired body measurements

Each timing worker retains one warmup cohort per arm and all six alternating
pairs: 1,078 outcomes, or 2,156 across both batch modes. Every cohort preserves
all 77 choices/rankings and 67 correct predictions, with no failures or unknown
outputs. Including confirmation, the increment retains 2,482 outcomes and
14,892 scores.

| Batch | Math cohort median | Efficient cohort median | Paired median | Paired p05 | Aggregate speedup | Efficient/math cohort p95 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1,292.955 ms | 1,224.230 ms | 1.056514 | 1.053600 | 1.056016 | 0.946585 |
| 8 | 907.924 ms | 852.400 ms | 1.065318 | 1.061005 | 1.065806 | 0.936997 |

Both modes pass all four prospectively declared speed gates. Six-observation
percentiles are descriptive, not confidence intervals. Canonical time sums
synchronized batch-body intervals including benchmark row bookkeeping;
ownership/source scans, quality checks, I/O and inter-call gaps are outside it.
Those gaps can still affect governor/cache state. Derived active-body service
rates do not establish observed unpaced throughput, queue latency or capacity.

The repeated-row batch-residence p95 has a separate result: **18.8981 to
19.2106 ms at B1** (a 1.6536% regression), versus **104.2367 to 98.7842 ms at B8**.
The exploratory B1 shape receipt retains all 77-by-six paired measurements.
Exactly four cases regress in every pair: the four longest inputs, at 197, 199,
203 and 214 tokens. Their 24 measurements form the entire candidate upper 5%
tail. No lengths 193–196 occur. Length association and a possible tile boundary
are hypotheses; no routing threshold or causal explanation is established.

## Cost observations and next tests

The independent profile-cost receipt preserves all four raw profiles. In the
representative efficient profiles, MLP matrix-operation self-device times account
for about 42.0% at B1 and 40.9% at B8 of captured kernel-duration sums. Packed
gate/up projections target about 29.0% and 27.2%, not all MLP work. Their
numerical behavior, GEMM tiling, transient/retained memory and complete latency
remain unknown. Fractions and ideal Amdahl ceilings apply only to explicitly
assumed serial captured event sums; missing stream information, profiling
interference and representative geometry prevent a cohort-wide bound.

The next narrow tail diagnostic compares real 192- and 197-token inputs with
actual kernel grids/durations and host gaps. A packed gate/up experiment is a
separate candidate. Neither observation releases a production policy. The
reference assay covers six-choice training-source menus with unknown exposure;
it establishes neither held-out Wyat quality nor the eventual export contract.
Production enablement also needs variable-count/length, causal, unsupported
kernel and resource/cancellation evidence. [The exact Torch 2.12.1 source](cuda/policy.md) supports process-wide
precision/backend ownership, including effective-versus-inherited precision
restoration limits. A dedicated fixed-policy worker remains a candidate;
per-application locking cannot isolate unrelated Torch clients.

## Receipts and resource bounds

Raw confirmations: `cuda-latency-confirm-b1.json` (`c41d4d08…`) and
`cuda-latency-confirm-b8.json` (`51a31cdd…`). Independent reviews:
`b25958e3…` and `067e0c36…`.

Raw timing: `cuda-latency-timing-b1.json` (`21ae0cc5…`) and
`cuda-latency-timing-b8.json` (`f72f3b8c…`). Independent reviews:
`790c0e5f…` and `90cf3e32…`. Exploratory shape receipt: `0d3f003a…`;
profile-cost receipt: `25a66296…`. All live in `benchmarks/analysis/results`.

Each independent raw audit runs under a 60-second owned cap without ML
frameworks, GPU access or networking. Executed source is archived unchanged;
the shape-analysis archive retains one harmless Ruff parenthesis finding.
The maintained increment passes 840 native CPU/Metal/DMBench tests with no
skips, strict mypy for 133 sources and Ruff for 139 files. Native regression
receipt: `engine-cuda-latency-verification.json` (`67930b46…`).

The four GPU workers finish in 20.750, 11.838, 71.126 and 25.654 seconds under
their respective 180-second caps. Owned parents/transports exit and reap;
final release observations at `2026-10-05T10:52:53Z` show 128 MiB, zero GPU
utilization, no compute applications and no owned latency worker. These are
instantaneous observations, not a reservation. The original 44 assets, seven
observer files, twenty production files and prior receipts remain unchanged;
no production default or artifact was published.

files.text:
# CUDA full77 confirmation and paired body latency

Prospective declaration, 2026-10-05. The engine task owns these bounded studies.
The corrected first-eight B1/B8 screen passes unchanged numerical and ranking
gates with observed FP32 efficient-attention kernels. Its independent audits
are `df30e1d4…` and `d474ea9d…`. This is evidence for progressing to the full
cohort; eight unique development cases establish neither full77 parity nor speed.

## Inputs, ownership and stages

Preserve the original 44-asset manifest `f7d9d7a4…`, original CUDA control
`d528a44e…` and its successful wall record `cb00f5f0…`, all twenty production
sources, and the seven-file observer declaration `589a45fe…` unchanged. Pin
both successful corrected screen receipts, their successful capped wall records
and exact source archives independently of the new source declaration. Root
has independently audited those raw screens; transferring their audit prose is
not required for runtime admission. Admit every original token, candidate
endpoint and query position across the full ordered 77-case cohort before GPU
allocation. Exact model, packages and CUDA build remain fixed.

Freeze the three new `cuda/latency` Python files, their focused test and this
document with a separate five-file declaration, checking bytes before and after
execution. Keep one loaded FP32 backbone/head owner, shared by the immutable
math scorer and the reviewed efficient-attention adapter. Use CPU threads eight,
maximum length 512 and token cache zero. No global attention registration,
weight duplication, model/config mutation or production policy change.

Use separate fresh, owned workers for confirmation and timing at each batch
mode (one and eight). Each worker has a 180-second whole-process cap. Fresh idle
observations before allocation and immediately before every batch stop foreign
compute ownership; never signal another job. Snapshots do not reserve hardware.
Restore IEEE/backend contexts and dispose observers before successful completion.
Retain partial rows, errors, pending case IDs, timeouts and cleanup/write failures.
No trial outcome or old source/archive is overwritten.

## Full77 confirmation

Run one ordinary math cohort and one ordinary efficient cohort on all 77 cases:
154 outcomes per batch mode. Validate each completed chunk against the aligned
original CPU reference and reviewed CUDA FP32 control before proceeding. Require
identical choices and full rankings, no accuracy loss or failed/missing/reordered
outputs, logit absolute/relative tolerance `1e-3` and probability tolerance `1e-4`.
Both ordinary cohorts must pass before representative profiling.

Profile only the first batch per arm afterward: two additional outcomes at B1,
sixteen at B8. Apply the same output gates. Use the immutable corrected observer:
expected public Q/K/V/mask/effective flags, private efficient and forward operator
counts, no fallback, and actual FP32 CUTLASS attention kernel evidence. Preserve
explicit-scale selector limitations, unknown converted-bias strides and internal
arithmetic uncertainty. Intrusive profiles support no ordinary latency claim or
cohort-wide Amdahl fraction. Any ordinary failure leaves profiles unstarted.

Independent raw confirmation review releases timing separately. Timing admission
must pin a complete, successful confirmation and parent wall record for its own
batch mode; a Boolean child flag alone is insufficient.
Timing's `dispatch_passed` describes that admitted representative confirmation
evidence; its explicit scope records that timed calls are unprofiled. It does
not assert contemporaneous dispatch observations for the timing cohorts.

## Ordinary paired timing

Run one complete warmup cohort per arm, then six pairs with order
`math/efficient, efficient/math` repeated three times. This is twelve measured
cohorts (924 outcomes) plus two warmups (154): exactly 1,078 outcomes per worker.
Preserve chronological orders and every raw chunk, warmup and measured result.
Check unchanged CPU/CUDA gates after every chunk and paired gates after each
complete pair. A quality, source or ownership failure aborts promptly; low speed
alone does not stop or select repetitions. B1 has 77 chunks per cohort; B8 has
nine full batches and a final batch of five, all in canonical order.

Canonical cohort latency is the sum of maintained synchronized
`_run(batch).latency_ms` intervals. This includes tokenization, batch packing,
model/backbone/head, host materialization, decision interpretation and benchmark
row bookkeeping. It excludes source admission, loading, warmup, ownership scans,
quality checks, JSON/file I/O, gaps between calls and HTTP transport/admission
queues. Request objects are prepared before timing. Retain batch residence
values separately; do not substitute their sum for the canonical metric.
Record actual complete-cohort and worker wall durations separately.

These are telemetry-paced synchronous batch-body measurements. Ownership scans
and gaps can affect arrival cadence, governor state and cache behavior even
though they are outside the timer. Active-body requests/second is a derived
service-rate diagnostic, not observed unpaced throughput or online capacity.
Neither body latency nor six-cohort percentiles establish online p95/p99 tails.
All timed calls must have no active Dispatch/profiler/diagnostic dtype hooks.

Declare a supported local gain only if all original quality/source/resource
conditions pass, with all six complete pairs, and all four speed gates pass:

- paired median speedup at least `1.05`;
- linearly interpolated paired p05 strictly greater than `1`;
- total baseline body time / total candidate body time strictly greater than `1`;
- candidate cohort p95 no greater than baseline cohort p95.

Percentiles from six observations are descriptive, not confidence intervals.
Report both batch modes separately; a win in one does not admit the other.
Keep every ratio, aggregate, negative and uncertainty. Loading/cross-device
changes are not a 20x same-device inference gain. These 77 training-source
menus remain a development runtime assay with unknown prior exposure, not
held-out Wyat quality or official BANKING77 evaluation. Production selection
requires separate review of the complete evidence and preserved public contracts.

## Cap feasibility observation

The read-only telemetry preflight at `2026-10-05T10:22:37Z` retained four
two-query ownership observations: 55.38, 37.06, 37.86 and 38.41 milliseconds.
Every query exited zero; the GPU showed 128 MiB, zero utilization and no compute
owner. Multiplying these samples by the planned check counts gives about
40–60 seconds at B1 (1,078 checks) and 5–8 seconds at B8 (140 checks), before
loading, inference, quality checks and persistence. This is a feasibility
estimate, not a wall-time bound or reservation. Keep the original 180-second cap.
Raw preflight: `cuda-latency-telemetry-preflight-20261005.json`.

# Fixed projection tile: source-level work account

Read-only audit, 2026-10-05. The initial custom tile remains frozen at
32×32×32, 128 threads. No device execution, model load or timing occurred in
this audit. These counts describe issued logical work, not measured DRAM
traffic, latency or an observed baseline kernel dispatch.

## Maintained comparison

The existing production receipt records Apple M4 Pro,
`applegpu_g16s`, MLX 0.32.3. In pinned
[matmul.cpp](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx/blob/64ea011cb65f14d9ce2737e60db9a4ae91ed7441/mlx/backend/metal/matmul.cpp),
ordinary Steel begins with BM=64, BN=64, BK=16, WM=2, WN=2. The
[architecture selection](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx/blob/64ea011cb65f14d9ce2737e60db9a4ae91ed7441/mlx/backend/metal/matmul.cpp)
retains these settings for the medium `s` device. `X @ W.T` selects the
nontransposed/transposed layout, with ready FP32 weights.

The [routing guard](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx/blob/64ea011cb65f14d9ce2737e60db9a4ae91ed7441/mlx/backend/metal/matmul.cpp)
requires NAX availability and either enabled TF32 or a non-FP32 input. The
assay sets `MLX_ENABLE_TF32=0` before import. Independently,
[device.cpp](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx/blob/64ea011cb65f14d9ce2737e60db9a4ae91ed7441/mlx/backend/metal/device.cpp)
requires generation ≥17 for the `s` architecture, excluding recorded g16s.
SIMD split-K also requires K≥max(M,N), false here because 1024<3072.
The source therefore predicts regular 64×64×16 Steel for these inputs.
An actual dispatch trace would be stronger evidence than this inference.

Installed header identities:

| Header | SHA256 |
| --- | --- |
| `steel/gemm/gemm.h` | `c84af31e2c57154f2a8a24fa7f9fe2449765cce9a66f3f035846ed3c03b6a8b0` |
| `steel/gemm/mma.h` | `9b37709de40c3acaa5411875e52c8d26e6de093261741f671fbdab9c39a852b7` |
| `steel/gemm/loader.h` | `c1b82153670b1e18371a6e88fdbcf440af692957775c2f837700315ab8a5112e` |

## Logical rereads and padded computation

For BM×BN output tiles, N=3072, K=1024 and exact tail admission, define
`gm=ceil(M/BM)`, `gn=ceil(N/BN)`. Valid operand-load bytes are
`4*M*K*gn` for X and `weight_itemsize*N*K*gm` for W; output stores are
`4*M*N`. This counts tile rereads, excluding cache effects, shared-memory
traffic, instruction overhead and allocator behavior. It differs from the
one-read minimum in [mixed.md](mixed.md).

| Shape | M | Custom 32 groups | Predicted Steel 64 groups | Custom BF16 X reads, bytes | Predicted Steel FP32 X reads, bytes | W reads, bytes, both paths |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Prefix B1 | 167 | 576 | 144 | 65,667,072 | 32,833,536 | 37,748,736 |
| Prefix B8 | 1336 | 4032 | 1008 | 525,336,576 | 262,668,288 | 264,241,152 |
| Full B1 | 192 | 576 | 144 | 75,497,472 | 37,748,736 | 37,748,736 |
| Full B8 | 1536 | 4608 | 1152 | 603,979,776 | 301,989,888 | 301,989,888 |

Our smaller output tile doubles both operand rereads. BF16 storage halves W
bytes, canceling only W's extra rereads. X remains FP32 and doubles. The
custom FP32 control has the same X rereads and twice the custom BF16 W bytes.
This gives the three-arm experiment a concrete way to separate storage
effects from tile-policy costs; none establishes physical traffic without
measurement.

Both tile policies pad prefix B1 to 192 rows and prefix B8 to 1344 rows.
Their mathematical padded FLOPs therefore match: 1,207,959,552 and
8,455,716,864. Full shapes need no row padding. Custom 32 uses four float8×8
accumulators per SIMD group; predicted Steel 64 uses sixteen. The total
number of 8×8×8 matrix accumulate operations is consequently equal for
each shape, despite four times as many custom threadgroups.

## One conditional follow-up

If the real screen admits all numerical gates but shows a slow primitive,
test output-tile reuse as one separately frozen hypothesis: 64×64×32,
128 threads, the same float arithmetic and BF16 local decoding. Keeping
M/N tile size equal to predicted Steel would halve our logical operand
rereads. K=1024 would use 32 reduction iterations rather than Steel's 64.
This does not predict a speedup: sixteen accumulators per SIMD group raise
register pressure, and keeping a separate float output staging tile would
raise shared storage from 12 KiB to 32 KiB. Occupancy, bank conflicts and
cache reuse remain unknown. A failed numerical screen requires numerical
diagnosis before any timing-oriented tile change.

The current custom tile executes 64 reduction-loop threadgroup barriers plus
one output barrier per group. Installed ordinary Steel executes 128
reduction-loop barriers for aligned K, additional synchronization and
direct fragment-to-device output stores. Barrier counts alone do not determine
runtime; the initial assay must finish before this follow-up is selected.

# Direct BF16 weight loads with FP32 projection arithmetic

Read-only orientation, 2026-10-05. Recommend one bounded primitive experiment,
not a production change. No framework import, model execution, kernel/JIT,
device probe or timing occurred during this investigation. Existing receipts
and the reserved CPU timing window remain untouched.

## Supported facility and present blocker

Installed MLX is 0.32.3. Ordinary `matmul` promotes both operands to a common
dtype, so FP32 activations plus BF16 weights materialize an FP32 weight operand
before multiplication. Its source and earlier storage audit are retained in
[storage.md](storage.md). This is the current promoted matmul baseline; it
already has FP32 weights and should not be charged a fictional per-call cast.

The maintained public [custom Metal API](https://ml-explore.github.io/mlx/build/html/dev/custom_metal_kernels.html)
generates each input pointer from that input's dtype, independently of output
dtype and template parameters. It can therefore accept FP32 X, BF16 W and
FP32 output. `ensure_row_contiguous` copies noncontiguous operands, preserving
their dtype. Its default safe math mode preserves special-value behavior;
it does not promise the same reduction order or bitwise matmul output.

The [0.32.3 custom evaluator](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx/blob/v0.32.3/mlx/backend/metal/custom_kernel.cpp)
binds those inputs directly and allocates the declared output dtype. Retrieved
Git blob: `b73dd72def76fa3412ef9155749507fe5d5cb48e`. The
[Python binding](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx/blob/v0.32.3/python/src/fast.cpp#L415)
passes the compile options through; blob:
`f9c472ab991cd156785c5323c0dea1818191e00d`.

Installed `bf16.h` defines `bfloat16_t` as Metal `bfloat`. Installed Steel
`mma.h` uses float SIMD fragments/accumulators and converts loaded elements to
the fragment type. However, its standard `BlockMMA` accepts the same storage
type T for both operands. A custom tiled kernel could convert BF16 weight
loads to float locally, then multiply float fragments, without a complete
FP32 W allocation. This is a feasible source-level hypothesis, not an existing
mixed-input matmul operator or verified fast kernel. Copying private Steel
implementation wholesale would add substantial maintenance surface.

[Apple's feature tables](https://developer.apple.com/metal/feature-sets/)
identify M4 as Apple9 and support BF16 scalar/vector values from Apple6.
They establish compatible loads, not doubled FP32 arithmetic throughput or
mixed-input matrix performance on this device.

Exact inspected installed files, relative to
`.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/mlx/`:

| File | SHA256 |
| --- | --- |
| `core/fast.pyi` | `e6ead453b46633174ef101388f4e6b7c02ed837fbee91db16aa3be39ea6f2d4b` |
| `include/mlx/backend/common/metal_kernel.h` | `b64ca4cebcba530d8ec1e0a0f23b57313507a37d05e3615ded3796b563cc83fc` |
| `include/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/bf16.h` | `abd87446a310b77ac530ef52a324feae5cb285d03ec9613e3a88ebb71410fdcb` |
| `include/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/steel/gemm/mma.h` | `9b37709de40c3acaa5411875e52c8d26e6de093261741f671fbdab9c39a852b7` |

The inspected production `wyat/backends/kai/mlx.py` SHA256 is
`2d56fa59c2fc0f04b6d9ba0fa210af1755ad8b265fead8b87a63505f140c8829`.

## One projection and conditional limit

Select only the first layer's real `gate_proj`: X[M,1024], W[3072,1024],
Y[M,3072], no bias. Capture the actual FP32 activation from the unchanged
checkpoint/encoder; do not substitute random tensors for the real observation.
The prefix job has full padded width 192 and fixed prefix 25, leaving suffix
width 167: M=167 at B1, M=1336 at B8. Full-prefill shapes are separately
M=192 and M=1536. Other batches may have different padded widths.
Before execution, token inspection selects case index 7 of the fixed first-eight
cohort for scalar capture because its encoded length is exactly 192. Batch eight
uses all eight cases, right-padded to 192. The scalar selection fixes geometry;
it is not a quality or timing selection. Observe the actual first-layer gate
input after attention separately for prefix and full-prefill execution.

W occupies 12 MiB in FP32 or 6 MiB in BF16. Admit BF16 storage only if decoding
it to FP32 reproduces every original finite weight's FP32 bits, including
signed zero. Never reduce activation precision. Arithmetic remains 2*M*1024*3072
FLOPs; the ideal one-read operand account is
`4*M*(1024+3072) + weight_bytes`.

| Execution shape | M | FLOPs | FP32 operand minimum, bytes | Mixed minimum, bytes | Traffic ratio |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Prefix B1 | 167 | 1,050,673,152 | 15,319,040 | 9,027,584 | 1.697 |
| Prefix B8 | 1336 | 8,405,385,216 | 34,471,936 | 28,180,480 | 1.223 |
| Full B1 | 192 | 1,207,959,552 | 15,728,640 | 9,437,184 | 1.667 |
| Full B8 | 1536 | 9,663,676,416 | 37,748,736 | 31,457,280 | 1.200 |

These are logical minima, not measured DRAM traffic or speed ceilings under all
cache conditions. Cache hits, tile rereads, workspace, weight-conversion work,
FP32 compute limits and dispatch overhead remain unknown. The likely limiting
tradeoff is reduced weight traffic versus conversion/tile occupancy and already
tuned FP32 compute, especially at B8. A half-sized W does not imply 2x runtime.

## Prospective bounded assay

After explicit resource release, freeze captured activation/weight bytes,
model/source identities, exact strides/shapes, kernel source, one tile policy,
compiler/math options and receipt schema before timing. Keep three arms:

1. Maintained FP32 `X @ W.T`, the current baseline.
2. One custom tiled FP32-input/FP32-weight/FP32-output kernel.
3. The same tile/arithmetic/reduction kernel with BF16 device weight loads
   converted to float locally; FP32 products, accumulator and output.

Use public Metal float SIMD matrix operations, safe math, disjoint output
ownership and no atomic reduction or reduced-precision intermediate. First
require a direct tiny boundary exercise of tail rows/columns, strides and
weight decoding. Reject unsupported layouts rather than silently timing copies.
The two custom storage arms must be bitwise equal on admitted real inputs;
both must be finite and satisfy elementwise
`abs(candidate-reference) <= 1e-4 + 1e-4*abs(reference)` against maintained FP32
matmul. Retain maximum errors and every failing element count. These are
prospective gates: do not loosen them after observing a failure.

Build each kernel once. Record capture, conversion, compilation, first dispatch
and cold allocation separately. After one warm dispatch per arm/shape, measure
six paired blocks, one for each permutation of the three arms, with ten
synchronized dispatches per arm/block, under a 512 MiB process cache cap. This
balances each arm's order position. Restore the original cap on exit;
retain before/after allocator snapshots outside timed intervals. Hold inputs
and weights ready in every arm. Use one owned child with a 180-second parent
bound; preserve incomplete/error receipts and release the model before primitive
timing. Preserve actual captured inputs, weights and cold outputs in an ignored
`*.tensors.safetensors` file. Check returned warm and timed outputs for bitwise
reproducibility against their own numerically admitted cold output after stopping
each interval; retain checks and failures. These intervening observations are
outside dispatch intervals and can perturb their surrounding execution. The
result does not establish unobserved back-to-back performance.
The proposed primitive success gate is median speedup >=1.05 and paired
p05 >1 against maintained matmul at both prefix shapes, with all numerical
gates passing. Full shapes are separately reported controls, not pooled wins.

A primitive pass would justify only a later single-projection integration
assay. That assay must retain the existing all-case CPU-reference gate:
logit atol/rtol 1e-3, probability absolute drift <=1e-4, exact candidate ordering,
selection and rank, failure-inclusive denominators. No end-to-end gain follows
from the primitive result; its production time fraction must be measured before
an Amdahl claim. No production interface, default change or kernel has been
introduced by this proposal.

## Completed fixed32 observation, 2026-10-05

The [real receipt](../../benchmarks/analysis/results/mlx-mixed-gate.json)
and [independent reconstruction](../../benchmarks/analysis/results/mlx-mixed-gate-review.json)
retain a completed negative result on Apple M4 Pro `applegpu_g16s`, MLX 0.32.3,
MLX-LM 0.31.3, FP32 arithmetic and `MLX_ENABLE_TF32=0`. The owned parent exited
1 after 9.816 seconds without reaching its 180-second timeout; the worker
completed the assay and rejected the prospective performance gate. The parent
`completed` flag records successful exit, so its false value does not make this
scientific observation incomplete. No production path changed.

Actual first-layer gate inputs were observed through the unchanged maintained
projection call during production prefix and full-prefill execution. Prefix
construction preceded observation; the exact original gate was restored after
each capture. Scalar captures used declared cohort index 7,
`banking77-train-03357`, whose original token length is 192. Batch captures used
the complete first eight cases. These four runs retained 18 decisions over eight
unique training-source cases, with 16 correct repeated decisions. Every selection,
complete ranking, logit and probability passed the frozen CPU reference gates;
maximum logit and probability errors were 1.45436e-5 and 1.59410e-6. This supports
execution preservation within this cohort, not held-out model quality.

All four captured inputs and the selected weight were materialized as independent
host-owned FP32 arrays before deleting model, head, prefix and observer owners.
The loader and prefix construction took 1,269.865 and 33.693 ms; capture plus
release took 2,062.913 ms. Input copy/materialization took 0.127–1.004 ms per
shape. The exact 12 MiB FP32 gate weight decoded from 6 MiB BF16 storage without
any bit mismatch. Weight reconstruction and BF16 conversion took 1.010 and
1.406 ms outside dispatch timing. The baseline held ready FP32 weights; no
recurring whole-weight conversion was charged to it.

All 12 cold outputs were finite and bitwise identical across the maintained,
custom FP32 and custom BF16 arms. Both custom arms passed 19,851,264 total
candidate-versus-reference element comparisons with zero maximum absolute error.
The separate independent FP64 `math.fsum` check covered 256 scalar dot products;
its largest absolute discrepancy was 3.91652e-6, within the declared bound. All
12 warm and 720 timed returned outputs reproduced their own cold output hashes.
The input/weight and cold-output Safetensors artifacts contain 25,817,488 and
119,108,704 bytes and remain ignored; hashes are retained in both receipts.

The table reports median ten-dispatch block means for each arm and the median
and p05 of six paired maintained/custom-BF16 block ratios. These quantities have
different denominators; the paired median is not a ratio of the displayed means.

| Actual shape | Maintained, ms | Custom FP32, ms | Custom BF16, ms | Paired median | Paired p05 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Prefix B1, M=167 | 0.494 | 1.015 | 0.905 | 0.5459 | 0.5092 |
| Prefix B8, M=1336 | 2.380 | 6.137 | 5.934 | 0.4010 | 0.3801 |
| Full B1, M=192 | 0.499 | 1.020 | 1.018 | 0.4963 | 0.4718 |
| Full B8, M=1536 | 2.680 | 7.644 | 7.419 | 0.3571 | 0.3493 |

Both prefix shapes failed the original median>=1.05 and paired-p05>1 gates.
Full-prefill shapes remain separate controls. Every raw dispatch, six balanced
arm permutations, block allocator snapshot and returned-output hash is retained.
Host copies, hashes and receipt writes occurred outside the dispatch intervals
and separate successive observations. Their surrounding cache/thermal effects
are unknown; these measurements do not establish unobserved steady throughput,
statistical significance, measured DRAM traffic or complete-inference speed.

After model release, MLX reported 20 active bytes and zero cached bytes. During
primitive blocks it reported 32,112,660 active and 52,297,760 cached bytes. Its
3,972,358,024-byte peak-active counter is cumulative across capture and projection,
not a primitive-body memory peak or physical RSS measurement. The 512 MiB
inactive allocator cache cap was restored to its original 24,481,313,587 bytes;
that cap is not a total-memory limit.

The [fixed source archive](../../benchmarks/analysis/results/mlx-mixed-gate.sources-94d1d0e80f80623c.json)
retains all 43 source files used by the assay. All current bytes matched at the
independent audit, before this result was appended. The archived prospective
`mixed.md` bytes intentionally precede this completed observation. The original
source archive, model/reference identities, raw inputs, outputs and timing
receipts remain unchanged. Independent audit SHA256:
`08d8b0bd6f60b8f24a2374a1ead6a43cc32d0228d10c77b3f714379314c9e985`.

Both custom storage arms are slower, so the observations do not isolate BF16
load conversion as the cause. The source-derived [tile work account](mixed-tile.md)
supports one separately frozen 64×64×32 reuse hypothesis: halve logical operand
rereads while accepting greater register and shared-memory requirements. Current
prefix-B8 BF16 latency would need approximately 2.62× improvement to satisfy the
1.05 gate. A wider tile is an unmeasured candidate, not an expected pass; any
follow-up must preserve these fixed32 artifacts and the numerical and performance
thresholds. No Amdahl or end-to-end speedup follows from this negative primitive.
