files.text:
# Measure scaling before choosing an optimization

The pure helpers in `benchmarks.analysis.scaling` summarize performance
hypotheses; observations determine whether those hypotheses hold. They have
no accelerator or optimization-library dependency. DMBench continues to own
general benchmark quality schemas, imports and scoring.

## Amdahl and roofline

For a fixed workload, accelerating a measured fraction `f` by factor `s`
predicts whole-operation gain `1 / (1-f + f/s)`. Removing that fraction gives
ceiling `1/(1-f)`. `amdahl_speedup` and `amdahl_ceiling` expose those quantities;
the latter returns `None` for the unbounded `f=1` case. This assumes unaffected
work and no new coordination cost. A synchronized diagnostic profile changes
execution, so its fractions yield conditional diagnostic ceilings rather than
promised end-to-end gains. The fixed-workload assumption follows the Amdahl
discussion in [Gunther's primary paper](https://arxiv.org/html/0808.1431v2#S2.SS1).

`roofline_lower_bound` returns the maximum of arithmetic work divided by
compute capacity and traffic divided by bandwidth. Its counts must be
justified work/traffic lower bounds and its rates justified hardware upper
bounds for the relevant precision. Operand bytes, tensor sizes and advertised
bandwidth do not establish measured DRAM traffic or sustained bandwidth.
Without those inputs, the runner records a roofline result as unknown.
Measurements below a proposed bound challenge its assumptions. The model
comes from [Williams, Waterman and Patterson's primary Roofline paper](https://aiichironakano.github.io/cs596/Williams-Roofline-CACM09.pdf).

The backbone arithmetic helper distinguishes hidden width `D`, query width
`Q = query_heads * head_dim` and KV width `K = kv_heads * head_dim`. Per-layer
projection FLOPs are `2 * tokens * [D*(Q+2K) + Q*D + 3D*I]`, where `I` is the
MLP intermediate width. A multiply-add counts as two FLOPs. Dense attention
adds `4 * batch * query_heads * length² * head_dim` per layer; ideal causal
triangular arithmetic instead uses
`2 * batch * query_heads * length*(length+1) * head_dim`. A fused causal
attention kernel's actual schedule remains unknown. These counts exclude
normalization, RoPE, softmax, nonlinear activations and the decision head.

The real model has `D=1024`, `Q=2048`, `K=1024`, `I=3072` and 28 layers.
Equating query width with hidden width would materially undercount its work.
Each batch reports original token count, padded count, width and padding
fraction. Counts describe the observed batching policy rather than implying
that padding can be removed from arbitrary model kernels without verification.

## USL is a diagnostic hypothesis

The user's [Universal Scaling Law collection](https://teilo.xyz/collections/universal-scaling-law/)
gives `C(N)=N/[1+sigma*(N-1)+kappa*N*(N-1)]`, with `0<=sigma<1`, `kappa>=0`.
It requires warmed steady-state data at six or more distinct loads and treats
the coefficients as diagnostic hypotheses. Its linked
[Gunther paper](https://arxiv.org/html/0808.1431v2#S2.SS3) derives the rational
capacity model and its peak `sqrt((1-sigma)/kappa)` when `kappa>0`.

`fit_usl` requires six unique loads including `N=1`. It normalizes measured
throughput by the observed load-one value, then fits `N/C(N)-1` to the two
columns `N-1` and `N*(N-1)` using a two-variable least-squares solution.
Parameters must satisfy the physical domain before a curve or peak is
admitted. Invalid estimates remain visible; they are never clipped to make
superlinear or otherwise incompatible measurements appear to fit the model.

The receipt retains raw throughputs, transformed residuals, raw throughput
residuals when a physical curve is admitted, capacity RMSE/R², maximum relative
error and normalized design conditioning. The transform weights errors
unequally and shares baseline uncertainty across every normalized point.
Correlated parameter columns can weaken identifiability. The current field
`normalized_gram_condition` is the eigenvalue ratio of the unit-column Gram
matrix; the normalized design condition is its square root. A Gram condition
above 100 generates a warning. The original receipt called this quantity
`normalized_design_condition`; its stored value is retained and interpreted
as a Gram condition. No confidence interval or mechanistic identification
follows from a small fitted curve.

A peak outside the observed load interval is explicitly marked as
extrapolation. Physical parameters alone cannot establish a useful fit:
capacity R² below 0.9 or maximum relative throughput error above 10% generates
a weak-fit warning. Those thresholds are illustrative diagnostics, not
predeclared quality or promotion gates, and cannot change the fitted
coefficients. Raw residuals remain visible even when the parameters pass.

Batch size changes amortization, matrix shape, padding and resource use; it is
not the processor/load-generator count assumed by the physical USL model.
The batch curve is explicitly descriptive. A decline with larger batches does
not establish cache coherence. Even a CPU thread curve would need to account
for the machine's heterogeneous performance/efficiency cores and investigate
the underlying contention rather than assigning a physical cause from a fit.

## Frozen six-shape development experiment

The first sweep uses every original case in the fixed 77-row BANKING77
training-source development cohort, unchanged caller order and the frozen
CPU FP32 reference. Its source-byte hash is
`0020d9a3c72a21941ba551cf31f404187f69c6a5dc30299cc0a24d303b904a03`.
Reference identity, original choice IDs, token IDs, candidate endpoints and
query positions must match before measurement. Released-model training
exposure remains unknown; this is no official or held-out benchmark score.

The six batch sizes are `1,2,4,8,16,32`. FP32, eager MLX GPU execution and zero
option-token cache remain fixed. Each shape receives one complete warmup and
six measured cohort cycles. Cyclic order rotation places every shape in every
order position once. The runner accepts multiples of six repetitions to
preserve that ordering balance. Setup, warmup, JSON persistence and HTTP are
excluded from timings. Native scorers materialize host floats synchronously.

Every warmup and measured shape must preserve all selections and full
rankings, logit absolute/relative tolerance `1e-3`, probability tolerance
`1e-4`, no failures and no labeled accuracy decrease against the same frozen
reference. All per-case logits, probabilities, rankings, exceptions and
timings remain in the receipt; measured cycles are also flushed to JSONL as
they complete. Failed calls cannot count as useful equivalent throughput.
Successful, equivalent and independently labeled-correct throughputs remain
separate. Repetition repeats the same 77 cases rather than increasing the
number of independent quality observations.

```sh
python -m benchmarks.analysis.run_scaling .models/Decision-2.0-Kai-0.6B
```

Complete-cohort length sorting, exact padding widths, packed projections and
CPU threading are separate hypotheses. They require their own measured
comparison and the same strict quality boundary before any production change.

## Observed first sweep and retained anomalies

The immutable [complete receipt](../../benchmarks/analysis/results/mlx-scaling77.json)
contains six measured cycles per shape, all successful with every selection
and full ranking preserved against CPU FP32. Each cycle classified 67/77 of
the independent labels correctly. Repetitions do not create additional
independent examples. The archived
[executed runner](../../benchmarks/archive/2026-10-05/scaling/run_scaling.txt)
and [executed helper](../../benchmarks/archive/2026-10-05/scaling/scaling.txt)
match its recorded source hashes. Subsequent typing, shared-reference cleanup
and diagnostic warning changes do not revise the measured receipt.

| Batch | Overall successful requests/s | Cohort p50 ms | Cohort p95 ms | Batch residence p95 ms | Padding fraction |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 13.94 | 5425.81 | 7484.21 | 84.02 | 1.67% |
| 2 | 11.41 | 3392.36 | 18767.63 | 158.15 | 3.83% |
| 4 | 23.71 | 3193.55 | 3584.96 | 263.95 | 5.22% |
| 8 | 25.12 | 3027.73 | 3358.76 | 431.99 | 7.82% |
| 16 | 24.32 | 3017.03 | 3564.90 | 926.78 | 10.15% |
| 32 | 25.53 | 2989.58 | 3142.49 | 1364.12 | 10.90% |

Residence describes an already-ready engine batch; it excludes any online
admission queue. Overall requests/s counts every timed cycle, including large
delays. Batch 32 is only 1.6% above batch 8 in overall throughput here and has
much higher batch residence. These observations do not support a general
batching recommendation before confirmation.

Batch 2's fifth measured round took 23817.93 ms; the slowest internal batch
took 18281.10 ms for `banking77-train-04562` and `banking77-train-01221`.
Batch 1's third round took 7999.86 ms; its slowest request,
`banking77-train-08638`, took 4295.68 ms. The former had no failures and 67
correct answers, as did its neighboring cycles. Cumulative process RSS stayed
2052882432 bytes before and after the cycle; that high-water measurement
cannot establish current device residency or diagnose a pause. This run did
not capture cycle wall timestamps, OS pressure or queue telemetry. The cause
of the delays is unknown, and no timing has been removed.

Later read-only system observations reported 15601.44 MB of swap in use out
of 21504 MB allocated and `memory_pressure -Q` free percentages of 16% then
26%. `pmset -g therm` reported no recorded warning; that does not establish
absence of throttling. These later observations cannot attribute the earlier
delays to pressure. Future confirmation should capture current swap, faults
and context switches around each cycle without changing unrelated apps.

The [posthoc sensitivity receipt](../../benchmarks/analysis/results/mlx-scaling77-sensitivity.json)
retains every original timing and binds the unchanged receipt and revised
analysis bytes by hash. The reciprocal-mean throughput fit has negative
`beta=-0.0000327805` and admits no physical USL curve. The reciprocal-median
fit has physical parameters but weak descriptive agreement: R² 0.8312,
maximum raw relative error 16.59%, and a predicted batch peak near 19.87.
Median timing describes a typical cycle rather than total capacity; changing
the summary statistic cannot accept the failed original fit or establish a
physical batching optimum. Gram condition is 55.0586, corresponding to design
condition 7.42015. Reproduce the separate analysis with:

```sh
python -m benchmarks.analysis.scaling_sensitivity \
  benchmarks/analysis/results/mlx-scaling77.json \
  benchmarks/analysis/results/mlx-scaling77-sensitivity.json
```

The [fresh five-pair batch-2/batch-8 confirmation](../../benchmarks/analysis/results/mlx-batch2-8-confirm77.json)
now preserves the same full cohort and strict FP32 quality boundary, with
all raw cycles and untimed system/device diagnostics. Median batch-8 speedup
is 1.165× with paired p05–p95 1.008–1.355× and one slower pair. Overall
requests/s is 22.65 versus 26.29. The default allocator retains 16.664 GB of
active-plus-cache allocation after continuous execution of these two shapes.
The [allocator study](cache.md) documents a separate controlled reset design
and its memory/throughput tradeoff. Neither experiment identifies the cause
of the original anomaly; the failed fit and all observations remain intact.

files.text:
# Server admission before threadpool dispatch

A valid concurrent decision request must receive 503 while this application's
model slot is occupied, including when AnyIO's shared pool is saturated.
Request-body limits, validation order, response schema, sanitized backend errors
and off-event-loop scoring retain their existing behavior. A started inference
continues owning its slot after HTTP cancellation until scoring actually exits.

## Counterexample and change

The previous server acquired its nonblocking model lock inside the worker.
Installed Starlette 1.7.0 delegates to AnyIO 4.15.1, which waits for capacity before
invoking that worker. A controlled HTTPX ASGI reproduction used one thread token
and an event-blocked scorer. Before release, a second request was queued with one
thread token borrowed and one waiter. After release, both requests returned 200
and the scorer ran twice, contradicting the documented concurrent-503 contract.
This is observed scheduling behavior; it needs neither a trained model nor a
network socket or timing-based throughput inference.

The handler now reserves the existing application gate before awaiting the pool.
One small per-request thread lock protects three states and their gate effects:

| Event | Prior state | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Worker claims admission | queued | running; worker owns the slot |
| Handler cancellation or dispatch failure | queued | released; free the slot |
| Handler exits while worker owns admission | running | retain worker ownership |
| Worker exits, including failure | running | released; free the slot |
| Late callback after withdrawal | released | reject before scoring; release nothing |

Every transition and release shares the same handoff critical section. The
handoff lock is never held through an await or scoring call. The app gate stays
reserved until its owner releases it; the short handoff lock protects that
ownership.
No scheduler, executor, global thread budget or model-arithmetic policy was added.

## Verification and limits

Five focused tests passed with actual capacity-one admission, cancellation before
worker start, late callbacks before and during another worker, and release after
submission/scorer failures. Twelve Hypothesis examples perturb cancellation and
callback counts and the two imposed handoff orders. They support these bounded
histories, not exhaustive scheduling proof. Existing started-worker cancellation,
validation, body limit and error tests remain unchanged; all fourteen pass.

The complete native CPU/Metal and actual DMBench regression passed **894 tests**,
zero skips and one existing Starlette/httpx deprecation warning. The owned pytest
child exited and was reaped in 67.712 seconds under its 120-second cap. Strict
mypy passed on 138 maintained files; Ruff lint and formatting passed. Sources
remained stable across checks. Only `wyat/server.py` changed among twenty runtime
files; all other 136 prior maintained sources remain unchanged.

Evidence: [typed counterexample](../../../benchmarks/analysis/results/server-admission-counterexample.json),
[owned reproduction](../../../benchmarks/analysis/results/server-admission-counterexample-wall.json),
[independent patch review](../../../benchmarks/analysis/results/server-admission-source-review.json),
[focused tests](../../../benchmarks/analysis/results/server-admission-focused-wall.json),
and [complete regression](../../../benchmarks/real/engine-server-admission-verification.json).
Initial reproduction/source-check rough edges and exact executed text are retained
separately, rather than overwritten. The patch supports admission correctness;
it establishes no HTTP capacity, online latency, model-quality or kernel speedup.

## Frozen inference evidence

Original CUDA declarations, raw runs, audits and source archives remain immutable.
The pending eight-file L192/L197 transfer does not include the changed server;
the remote twenty-file runtime remains its original frozen snapshot. Its source
identity must be checked against those exact archives, rather than requiring the
current checkout to stay byte-identical forever. The former 889-test receipt is
historical; the new 894-test receipt describes the current server. No new private
payload transfer or CUDA job has occurred while authorization remains pending.

# Prospective CUDA tail diagnostic

Declaration, 2026-10-05. The independent [ordinary timing results](latency-results.md)
support a modest B1 cohort-body gain but show a 1.6536% repeated-row residence
p95 regression. All six pairs regress for the four longest development inputs
at 197, 199, 203 and 214 tokens; the remaining maximum is 192, with 193–196
unobserved. Those associations do not establish a cause or a routing threshold.

Hypothesis: a launch-geometry boundary between the actual 192- and 197-token
inputs contributes to the observed regression. The diagnostic does not assume
a query tile or grid size from `64x128` in an attention kernel's name.

## Frozen inputs and ownership

Use exactly `banking77-train-03357`, the first canonical 192-token case at
offset 7, and `banking77-train-00566`, the sole 197-token case at offset 18.
Select from the pinned CPU-reference encodings before new captures. Preserve
every token, candidate ID, endpoint, query position and input order across the
full original 77 cases before loading weights or allocating CUDA tensors. No
replacement, text alteration, padding-width search or synthetic input is admitted.

Keep unchanged the original 44 assets (`f7d9d7a4…`), CUDA FP32 main/control wall
(`d528a44e…` / `cb00f5f0…`), corrected observer seven (`589a45fe…`), latency five
(`a26d5be4…`) and 48-source execution archive (`21b3fa50…`). Admit the exact B1
confirmation main/wall (`c41d4d08…` / `29d7fe3a…`), its independently reconstructed
full77 quality/source/dispatch evidence, and the separately pinned timing and
exploratory shape evidence. Old receipts and declarations remain immutable.

Freeze three new `cuda/shape` Python files, `test_cuda_shape.py` and this document
in a separate five-file declaration. Transfer those files, their declaration,
and the two already reviewed timing/shape-association JSONs: eight files total.
The latter two are immutable admission evidence, separately pinned rather than
new execution sources. Use the existing engine workspace only after independent
source/test review.
Retain the new executed source archive separately from prior sources.

One fresh worker owns one FP32 backbone/head, shared by math and the reviewed
efficient adapter. Use threads eight, maximum length 512, token cache zero,
full prefill without KV cache, disabled autocast and IEEE global/matmul settings.
No registration, backbone duplication, production policy or default changes.
The parent caps only its owned worker group at 180 seconds. Fresh ownership
checks before allocation and each call reject foreign jobs; source/history
checks, persistence and ownership scans sit outside ordinary body clocks and
captures. Idle observations are not reservations.

## Fixed schedule and gates

For each phase, use exactly this order: L192 math, L192 efficient, L197 efficient,
L197 math. Run phases warmup, ordinary, then profile: **four warmup, four ordinary
and four profiled outcomes**, twelve total. Profile neither shape before all
ordinary outcomes pass. Compare every completed result with its aligned CPU
and CUDA references and same-case arm: identical choice/full ranking, no failed
or missing result, no accuracy decline, original `1e-3` absolute/relative logit
and `1e-4` probability gates. Low or high latency never selects observations.

Ordinary synchronized body/residence and phase/worker walls are retained
separately. Four ordinary controls cannot establish a speed gain or tail estimate;
the original six-pair results remain the independent speed evidence. No new
speed gate or production admission rule is introduced.

Capture each shape/arm once in its own CPU+CUDA profiler context with
`record_shapes` and the immutable public Dispatch observer. Label each call
explicitly with arm, case and actual length. Synchronize before capture and
after its sole call before closing the context. Export each ended context to a
distinct exclusive Chrome JSON under the output's owned `.trace` directory,
which existing packaging exclusions omit. Preserve exact bytes, SHA, size and
path; exporting a scheduled profiler's last cycle alone is insufficient.

Require unchanged efficient evidence at each actual length: 28 public Q/K/V/mask
and effective-flag observations, 28 private efficient/forward calls, no fallback
and 28 actual FP32 SM80 attention kernels. Retain the math comparator's actual
math/no-efficient evidence. Keep explicit-scale selector limitations, converted
bias strides and internal arithmetic unknowns. IEEE matmul and FP32 tensors do
not establish IEEE attention arithmetic.

## Native trace interpretation

Store the complete native traces before designing a schema interpreter. Preserve
each event's original index, phase/category/name, process/thread IDs, timestamp,
duration and entire arguments. Actual grid, block, stream, device and correlation
fields may be missing or malformed; retain those as unknown, without filling
them from tensor dimensions or kernel names.

Independent review links a kernel to a same-trace runtime launch by a unique,
exactly typed correlation value, then to a CPU operation by unique External ID
where observed. Missing or multiple matches remain unknown. Correlation and
External ID are distinct. Do not match by name, order or timestamp proximity.

Chrome timing, Python performance clocks and UTC remain separate domains unless
an observed clock mapping supports a comparison. Kernel-event sums count each
event once, separate from inclusive CPU/runtime durations. Per-stream gaps,
interval unions and spans are descriptive when metadata is present; they do
not prove a critical path, host-launch bottleneck or device occupancy.

- Identical complete grid/block distributions across all 28 efficient kernels
  challenge the proposed grid/block step for this pair. Other internal loop,
  alignment, layout or algorithm boundaries remain unknown. If multiple geometries
  occur, equal multisets leave a possible per-layer permutation unknown. Stronger
  refutation requires one uniform geometry in both captures or independently
  linked corresponding layers; event order and whole-case labels do not establish
  layer identity.
- Different observed geometry establishes a geometry change only. Attention
  duration changes relative to the math comparator and remaining operations may
  support a contribution; content/menu, capture order, governor state and
  intrusive-observer effects remain confounded.
- Missing geometry or linkage leaves the mechanism unknown. Dominant changes
  in other matrix/copy operations or host-visible spans challenge attention as
  the useful next target, without themselves establishing causation.

Retain all attempted and unstarted IDs, partial rows, warnings, failed exports,
timeouts, context/observer cleanup and final-write failures. Positive completion
requires all source/history rechecks and cleanup; `accepted` remains false.
Independent raw audit and terminal GPU/job-release observations follow capture.
This diagnostic supports no online tail/capacity, held-out model quality, 20x
gain, routing threshold or production promotion. A controlled synthetic length
perturbation, if needed, requires its own declaration.

files.text:
# Exact 16-bit weight storage with FP32 computation

Read-only source audit on 2026-10-05. No maintained MLX 0.32.3 matmul path was
found that directly reads BF16 weights while preserving FP32 activations,
products and accumulation. The ordinary path explicitly promotes the weights
to FP32. This is a concrete blocker to treating smaller stored weights as a
demonstrated DRAM-traffic optimization. No kernel, installation, model execution
or hardware measurement was performed; historical receipts remain unchanged.

## What the source establishes

The inspected version is the `v0.32.3` release tag. In
[`mlx/ops.cpp`, lines 3513–3527](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx/blob/v0.32.3/mlx/ops.cpp#L3513),
`matmul` selects one promoted dtype and inserts `astype` for either operand
that differs. FP32 activations with BF16 weights therefore create an FP32
weight operand before `Matmul`. The retrieved Git blob is
`83094d25b827c0a395b47ce31402fdd048b6fd9e`.

The standard
[`Steel GEMM`](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx/blob/v0.32.3/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/steel/gemm/gemm.h#L23)
has input type `T`, output type `U` and accumulation type; both A and B loaders
use the same `T`. Its
[`BlockLoader`](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx/blob/v0.32.3/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/steel/gemm/loader.h#L38)
uses that same type for device and threadgroup memory. `U` is not an independent
weight-input dtype. The
[`BlockMMA`](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx/blob/v0.32.3/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/steel/gemm/mma.h#L439)
default accumulation type is float; that alone does not preserve FP32 inputs
when both operand loaders use BF16. Retrieved GEMM/loader/MMA blobs are
`bbe1d96cc0a657e729b2be8a0808382886866ba0`,
`c999fdc91acad1903ff824b36a7e9ca9c7b57675` and
`1d9e0a7820f1eee9276f7ff23cf96bcd5b8bdae5`.

`qqmm` does accept a non-quantized weight argument, but its
[`Metal implementation`](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx/blob/v0.32.3/mlx/backend/metal/quantized.cpp#L2107)
quantizes that argument and quantizes/dequantizes activations. It is not a
lossless BF16-storage pass-through. `quantized_matmul` requires encoded weights
and scales: a separate quantization recipe whose exact weight reconstruction
and arithmetic would need verification. Output dtype alone cannot waive that
contract. The retrieved quantized implementation blob is
`97c418e872a5f21a6ae16522727ab8a853036976`.

Apple's [feature tables](https://developer.apple.com/metal/feature-sets/)
list BF16 scalar/vector support and SIMD matrix operations for the M4's Apple9
family. This does not establish a public MLX mixed-input operator or its
numerical parity. A custom BF16 device load followed by FP32 conversion inside
a tile is a plausible kernel technique, not an inspected maintained path.

The existing [tiny graph probe](../../benchmarks/analysis/results/mlx-mixed-storage.executed.py)
stores **FP16** weights built from BF16-representable source values. Its
`AsType`/FP32 matmul observation is consequently FP16-specific. The source
promotion rule above independently establishes the BF16 case; no BF16 GPU
measurement is inferred from that probe.

## Dimensions and conditional traffic ceiling

For the present checkpoint, a projection is `X[M,K] @ W[N,K].T`, where
`M=batch × padded_tokens`. Preserve FP32 X/output, every original weight value,
causal positions and the candidate head.

| Projection | Weight shape | FP32 bytes | BF16 bytes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Q | 2048 × 1024 | 8 MiB | 4 MiB |
| K and V, each | 1024 × 1024 | 4 MiB | 2 MiB |
| O | 1024 × 2048 | 8 MiB | 4 MiB |
| Gate and up, each | 3072 × 1024 | 12 MiB | 6 MiB |
| Down | 1024 × 3072 | 12 MiB | 6 MiB |

That is 15,728,640 projection elements per layer: 60 MiB FP32 versus 30 MiB
BF16; across 28 layers, 1,680 versus 840 MiB. Embeddings, norms, head and
workspace are excluded. Packed QKV is 4096 × 1024, not 3072 × 1024; packed
gate/up is 6144 × 1024. Packing does not change this element count.

If every projection weight were read once from DRAM per batch, direct 16-bit
loads would halve that **weight** traffic. Real cache reuse, tile rereads,
activations, outputs and other operators invalidate any automatic whole-engine
2× claim. The ideal ceiling is 2× for time entirely due to those weight reads;
with measured fraction `f`, the conditional total ceiling is
`1 / (1 - f/2)`. That fraction and actual DRAM traffic are unknown. Materializing
the existing cast may instead require reading 2 bytes, writing 4 and later
reading 4 per element; this 10-byte account is conditional on materialization
and excludes cache effects, not measured traffic.

## Narrow hypothesis and stopping boundary

A future kernel could decode exact BF16 weights to FP32 in registers or
threadgroup tiles, retain FP32 X and the maintained FP32 MMA/reduction policy,
and eliminate the full FP32 weight intermediate. It would require changing
the loader/kernel and dispatch contract; a Python dtype switch cannot do it.
BF16 storage is admissible only after exact FP32 round-trip checks per tensor.
Changed reduction order still requires strict numerical gates.

Before implementation, establish a measured weight-traffic/launch bottleneck
and an affected-time ceiling. If pursued, first test the actual rectangular
projection shapes and tail M, then the frozen full cohort, retaining rank,
selection, logit/probability drift and synchronized complete-request time.
Reject the hypothesis if cast buffers persist, precision gates fail or measured
complete-request benefit is absent. No maintained implementation or performance
claim is established by this audit.

files.text:
# Diagnose the 64-tile regression before selecting another optimization

Research note, 2026-10-05. No Metal compiler, GPU dispatch, capture or replay
ran during this investigation. Existing kernels, protocols and historical
receipts remain unchanged.

## Observation and competing explanations

The [real 64-tile receipt](../../benchmarks/analysis/results/mlx-tile64-gate.json)
preserves numerical agreement but fails performance selection. Median stock
over 64-tile ratios are 0.181669 at prefix B1 and 0.148303 at prefix B8.
The corresponding 32-tile over 64-tile ratios are 0.372923 and 0.363842.
Output reuse therefore did not compensate for other costs in this implementation.

The source changed several resource demands together: four accumulators per
SIMD group became sixteen; shared storage increased from 12 KiB to 32 KiB;
shared W scatter stride increased from 32 to 64; fewer threadgroups perform
more work each. Both bodies use constant-trip fragment loops with
source-variable array indices and no explicit unroll annotation. The compiler
may already turn these into static accesses. Timing does not establish spills,
occupancy loss, bank conflicts or the executed instruction sequence.

## Public compiler boundary and one source perturbation

Pinned MLX 0.32.3's
[Python binding](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx/blob/64ea011cb65f14d9ce2737e60db9a4ae91ed7441/python/src/fast.cpp)
accepts only `math_mode` in `compile_options`; unknown keys raise an error.
The [custom evaluator](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx/blob/64ea011cb65f14d9ce2737e60db9a4ae91ed7441/mlx/backend/metal/custom_kernel.cpp)
gets a pipeline through Metal and checks its maximum threadgroup size.
Neither Python surface exposes register counts, spill bytes, an unroll option
or Apple's library optimization level. The underlying
[MTLCompileOptions](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/metal/mtlcompileoptions)
supports optimizer settings, but that does not make them available through MLX.

Installed maintained Steel uses `_Pragma("clang loop unroll(full)")` in
`.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/mlx/include/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/steel/defines.h`,
line 6, SHA256
`b03cea6a7d5cfe814e6838d8536e2aacdcafd2744cb408e954fda336ce21759a`.
Its `steel/gemm/mma.h` applies this to fragment operations. Apple's
[Metal Compute guidance](https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/tech-talks/10580/)
connects dynamic stack-array indexing with possible spills and recommends
compile-time indices. This supports a hypothesis, not a diagnosis of our kernel.

If diagnostics justify a perturbation, explicitly request full unrolling only
for the constant fragment initialization, inner K8 iteration, fragment load,
row/column accumulate and fragment store loops. Keep outer K32 traversal,
tile size, shared layout, safe math, dtype, tails and arithmetic order fixed.
[Clang documents](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/LanguageExtensions.html#loop-unrolling)
the pragma as an optimization request, so successful compilation would not
prove static indices or absence of spills. Increased live values or code size
could make it slower. No annotation or generated expansion is implemented here.

## Minimal decisive measurement

Full Xcode is selected locally. Read-only path discovery resolved `metal` and
`xctrace`; their execution and profiler compatibility are untested. The
installed `mlx/core/metal.pyi` exposes `start_capture` and `stop_capture`;
SHA256 `aecdeb33b024ad2096af9e8e584c679bbdd05d375770418351cbea410353b2b9`.

Within a coordinated resource window, reuse the frozen real input
bytes and prepare both existing kernels before capture. Set
`MTL_CAPTURE_ENABLED=1` and `MLX_ENABLE_TF32=0` before importing MLX. Use public
`mx.metal.start_capture` with a fresh `.gputrace` path, evaluate and synchronize
one ready dispatch from each policy, then stop capture in `finally`. Keep
model loading, layout probes, first compilation and capture outside benchmark
timing. Use an owned bounded process; preserve any incomplete trace/error and
release its resources.

[MLX's debugger workflow](https://ml-explore.github.io/mlx/build/html/dev/metal_debugger.html)
supports opening and replaying the trace in Xcode. It describes
`MLX_METAL_DEBUG` builds for source recording and labels; the installed build's
source visibility is unknown. A capture file alone is not profiling evidence.
Replay with profiling enabled and inspect each pipeline's compiler statistics,
including reported spill bytes and threadgroup memory, plus measured occupancy.
[Apple's profiling workflow](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/xcode/analyzing-apple-gpu-performance-using-counter-statistics)
distinguishes captured commands from collected profiling metrics.

To separate explanations, inspect source-correlated memory costs where available.
Spill bytes and stack/register traffic would support the array-index hypothesis;
expensive shared staging with little reported spilling would favor a shared-layout
perturbation. Low occupancy alone is insufficient. Apple's
[family 9 tools](https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/tech-talks/111374/)
expose occupancy-management, L1 eviction, residency and bandwidth counters for
this investigation. These counters can reflect several memory owners, so retain
their breakdown and uncertainty rather than labeling all L1 traffic as spills.
Availability, replay permissions, metric export and a usable source view remain
unverified; missing observations stay unknown.

Any subsequent unroll or transpose assay needs its own prospective source and
protocol freeze. Preserve the original 32 and 64 paths as controls, repeat
bitwise storage/control checks and the existing elementwise numerical gate,
and keep the same paired performance thresholds and failure denominators.
Profiled timings must not replace the uninstrumented selection measurements.

# Output reuse trial

This declaration precedes the fixed64 real-tensor experiment. The operational
owner is the Wyat engine task. Both kernels remain experimental; frozen32 is a
live control for the previously rejected implementation. Neither is selected for
production. Keep the prior receipts, captured tensors and executable sources
unchanged so the comparison can be reproduced.

Hypothesis: changing the output tile from 32×32 to 64×64, with the same 32-element
reduction order and independently decoded BF16 weights, can reduce repeated
input and weight reads enough to improve the first-layer gate projection. The
larger tile uses 32KiB shared storage and 16 float matrix accumulators per SIMD
group, compared with 12KiB and 4. Register pressure, occupancy and physical memory
traffic are unknown. Logical read counts are predictions, not profiler results.
The source account is in [mixed-tile.md](mixed-tile.md).

Admit the exact previous main receipt `fb8bde4a…`, independent audit `08d8b0bd…`
and tooling verification `e332f2fa…`, including their complete source archives,
model identity, dataset, CPU reference, captured activation/weight file and cold
outputs. The sole admitted historical document difference is the exact audited
result append to `mixed.md`; executable bytes remain frozen. Read the actual
captured inputs at M=167, 1336, 192, 1536, K=1024 and N=3072. Do not recapture a model,
substitute data, or pool prefix and full-input shapes.

Before timing, reproduce the prior maintained and frozen32 cold output bits.
Require finite outputs within `1e-4 + 1e-4 * abs(reference)` for each candidate
element against maintained FP32. Require the new64 BF16 and new64 FP32 cold
outputs to agree bitwise, including the tiny signed-zero and arbitrary-FP32
input tests. Store all four arms' cold arrays. Numerical admission precedes
performance measurement.

Time three arms: maintained FP32, frozen32 BF16, and new64 BF16. Use all six
permutations, ten separately synchronized dispatches per arm and block, and one
warm dispatch per arm at each of the four shapes. Include dispatch, evaluation
and synchronization in each interval. Hash every warm and timed output outside
its timer against that arm's cold output. Those observations may perturb later
dispatches; this measures observed dispatches, not uninterrupted throughput.

The unchanged success gate compares new64 with maintained: the median of six
paired block ratios must be at least 1.05 and their interpolated fifth percentile
must exceed 1, at **both prefix shapes**. Report full-input controls separately.
New64 versus frozen32 is descriptive evidence about this hypothesis; improvement
over the rejected kernel does not establish an improvement over maintained
MLX. Do not relax thresholds or select a favourable shape after seeing results.

The parent remains framework-free and owns one worker with a 180-second deadline,
process-group cleanup and terminal wall receipt. Disable TF32 before MLX import,
use the GPU stream, and restore the prior allocator-cache limit after applying
512 MiB during the trial. This cache setting does not cap resident memory. Save
completed arms and preserve partial/error receipts; an interrupted arm remains
unknown. Archive exact trial sources before execution. Independent review and
tiny correctness checks precede the real run. DMBench has reserved this bounded
window; unrelated applications' activity is not established.

A projection result cannot establish complete-inference latency, held-out model
quality, or a 20× engine improvement. Any selected kernel would need a separate
complete-inference experiment under the existing logits, probabilities, full
ranking and performance gates.

# Observe the compiled projection

Prospective diagnostic, 2026-10-05. The Wyat engine task owns the bounded
capture/replay. This is separate from latency selection. DMBench has standing
compute availability until it reports a conflict; unrelated application load
is unknown.

Reuse the admitted real prefix batch-eight activation `[1336,1024]` and gate
weight `[3072,1024]`. Prepare the frozen32 and frozen64 kernels, decode BF16
weights locally, and validate their cold outputs against the archived exact
outputs before capture. Do not allocate a model or recapture activations.

Set `MTL_CAPTURE_ENABLED=1` and `MLX_ENABLE_TF32=0` before importing MLX. Capture
one ready GPU dispatch for each kernel into separate fresh `.gputrace` bundles.
Synchronize explicitly and stop each started capture in `finally`. Apply a
512 MiB allocator-cache limit and restore its prior value and the parent environment;
retain errors and
partial artifacts, and reap only owned processes under a hard deadline. Keep
first compilation, admission and output observation outside capture. Record the
actual deadline and ownership outcome in the receipt.

The installed `gpudebug` manual documents `--oneshot`, structured JSON output
and `profile run --exec serial --gpu-state default` on M3/A17 or later devices.
Try a separately bounded one-shot replay of each bundle, without embedding
profiling into or changing the original capture. Inspect actual compiler and
performance fields for spill bytes, occupancy and memory costs. Preserve raw
tool output and observed variation; do not invent absent fields or infer
compiler spills from timing alone. A captured bundle is not itself evidence of
spills or occupancy.

The offline `xcrun metal --help` currently fails because the Metal Toolchain
component is absent. Installed `xctrace` works, but the previous trace explicitly
disabled shader timing and had no counter set. That old shader inventory cannot
answer this diagnostic. No component download is needed to try the maintained
public MLX capture and installed replay interface.

Raw capture bundles contain model/input buffers: keep them Git-ignored and
excluded from the source distribution. Sanitized receipts describe provenance
and diagnostic observations. Replayed/profiled timing does not replace the
existing four-shape, six-order uninstrumented numerical/performance gates. The
explicit fragment-loop-unrolling candidate remains a separate hypothesis under
[unroll.md](unroll.md).

files.text:
# Constant fragment loops

Prospective declaration, 2026-10-05. The Wyat engine task owns this experimental
increment. The previous fixed32 and fixed64 sources and receipts remain frozen
controls; production is unchanged.

Hypothesis: explicit full unrolling of the fixed64 kernel's constant fragment
loops can improve its real gate-projection dispatches. Apple's
[Metal compute guidance](https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/tech-talks/10580/)
describes possible register spills from dynamically indexed arrays. Maintained
Steel uses a Clang full-unroll pragma. These sources motivate the perturbation;
they do not establish that our compiled kernel spills or that unrolling helps.

Change only constant fragment initialization, K8 iteration, fragment loading,
row/column matrix accumulation and fragment stores. Preserve the outer K32
traversal, 64×64 output tile, 128 threads, 32 KiB shared storage, shared layouts,
safe math, operand types, BF16 local decoding, reduction order and tail bounds.
Do not combine this with transposed shared loads or direct output stores.

Admit the previous fixed64 main receipt `22dcca46…`, independent audit
`9099425d…`, tooling verification `966ba6a3…`, their exact source archives and the
original fixed32 evidence. Reuse the exact captured real X/W file `70f0245d…`.
Require the model, data and CPU-reference identities before importing the device
framework. No model recapture or substitute activations are allowed.

Before timing, reproduce maintained and frozen64 cold output bits, at all four
shapes: M=167, 1336, 192, 1536; K=1024; N=3072. Require every finite candidate
output within `1e-4 + 1e-4 * abs(reference)` against maintained FP32. Require the
unrolled kernel's FP32/BF16 cold outputs to agree bitwise. Tiny tests separately
cover arbitrary FP32 activations, low bits, signed zeros, tails and layout
rejection. Save all cold outputs, including the FP32 storage control.

Time three arms: maintained FP32, frozen64 BF16 and unrolled64 BF16. Use all six
permutations, ten separately synchronized dispatches per arm/block, and one warm
dispatch per arm/shape. Include dispatch, evaluation and synchronization inside
each interval. Hash every warm/timed output outside its timer against its own
cold output. This observation may perturb later dispatches; it does not measure
uninterrupted throughput.

Success still requires maintained/unrolled paired median at least 1.05 and
interpolated fifth percentile greater than 1 at **both prefix shapes**. Keep
full-input controls separate. Frozen64/unrolled is descriptive evidence of the
perturbation, not a promotion gate or a substitute for beating maintained MLX.
Retain all orders, failures and variation; do not revise thresholds after data.

Use a framework-free parent and one owned worker capped at 180 seconds. Disable
TF32 before MLX import, use the explicit GPU stream, restore the parent environment
and the allocator-cache limit after applying 512 MiB, and reap only owned
processes. The cache setting is not a total-memory bound. Preserve completed
arms, partial/error receipts and late-write failure status. Archive exact
sources before dispatches; independent source review and native tiny/fake checks
precede the real trial.

Any GPU capture is a separate diagnostic artifact with a separate bounded
owner. Profiled/replayed timing cannot replace this uninstrumented comparison.
Compiler spill counts, occupancy and physical memory traffic remain unknown
until directly observed. A projection win would still require a complete-engine
quality and latency confirmation before production selection.

Pre-run diagnostic limit: the documented `gpudebug` replay attempt timed out
without producing compiler or performance fields. Its owned client was killed
and reaped; no matching replay process was visible afterward, while hidden XPC
session state remains unknown. Capture workers and native correctness tests were
terminal before timing. The result retains this uncertainty and does not claim
physically exclusive compute or a demonstrated register-spill mechanism.

files.name: docs/dmbench-integration.md
files.text:
# Use a loaded Wyat model with DMBench

Wyat owns model loading and inference. DMBench owns benchmark imports, case
schemas, provenance, groups, expected answers and quality scoring. Wyat's
`benchmark_pair` is an engine performance and parity experiment; use DMBench
for general benchmark quality evaluation.

Install both projects in the same environment. DMBench is optional; importing
Wyat or its adapter does not import DMBench. The adapter imports DMBench when
`as_dmbench` is called and reuses the already-loaded model for every request.

```python
from dmbench import evaluate
from dmbench.io import load_cases

import wyat
from wyat.interop.dmbench import as_dmbench, as_dmbench_batch

model = wyat.load("/local/kai-bundle", device="cpu")
cases = load_cases("/local/dmbench-dataset")
report = evaluate(
    cases,
    as_dmbench(model),
    batch=as_dmbench_batch(model),
    batch_size=8,
)
```

The default adapter recipe, `dmbench-verbatim-choice-v1`, places DMBench's
`Request.text` verbatim in the Wyat query and
leaves context empty. Each supplied choice becomes a candidate with the exact
same ID, description and order. DMBench task names identify benchmark panels;
the Wyat request uses `task="choice"` to identify its inference contract.
Source IDs, groups, splits and expected answers are never placed in the model
input.

`as_dmbench` preserves the scalar callable boundary. `as_dmbench_batch` calls
the loaded model's native `decide_many` once per ordered chunk; neither helper
spawns concurrent model calls. They share the same request and prediction
conversions. Empty tuples return empty tuples without inference. A choiceless
member rejects its whole chunk before the model is called. DMBench retains
chunk failures and records the true batch wall time; it does not fabricate
per-item timing by dividing the batch duration. Omit `batch` and `batch_size`
for scalar evaluation.

The default recipe adds no serializer. The selected Wyat backend alone owns
its prompt recipe. A benchmark text may contain JSON, embedded instructions,
context or choices; the default recipe does not parse, strip or reconstruct
that text. Benchmark authors select other projections explicitly in their
model factory.

The opt-in `dmbench-native-choice-v1` recipe accepts only the explicit
`jevbench/choice` task and DMBench's native `question.type="choice"` schema:

```python
recipe = "dmbench-native-choice-v1"
report = evaluate(
    cases,
    as_dmbench(model, recipe=recipe),
    batch=as_dmbench_batch(model, recipe=recipe),
    batch_size=8,
)
```

It delegates schema admission to DMBench's actual
`dmbench.adapters.native.native_request`. That helper checks exact
state/question/labels roles, task/type agreement, label/menu order and
criterion/menu text agreement. Wyat puts `question.instructions` verbatim
in the query. A string state becomes context verbatim; object or conversation
list state becomes context through DMBench's `canonical_json`, preserving
typed JSON values and list order. Public choices retain their exact IDs,
text and order. The envelope and criteria are not appended again to the
query. No heuristic envelope detection or independent parser is introduced.

Recipe selection is validated when constructing the callable. Scalar and
batch projections use the same conversion, and the entire public chunk is
validated before calling the loaded model. A missing or unknown native role,
criterion mismatch, unsupported task or task/type mismatch rejects the chunk.
JevBench `noul` and ordinal `score` remain unsupported by this choice recipe.
DMBench's native validator is imported only when the native path is used;
module import and the default path retain their existing optional-dependency
behavior. Recipe identity belongs in the model factory/evaluation provenance;
the selected recipe is never inferred from benchmark text.

The result answer is the selected original choice ID. Optional probabilities
are the loaded model's native choice softmax values mapped to those IDs; they
are relative scores, not calibrated correctness estimates. Token counts and
forward-pass counts remain unknown, so usage is omitted. Inference exceptions
propagate to DMBench, whose evaluator retains failed cases in its denominator.

A choice head requires supplied choices. Open answers, JevBench ordinal scores
and the frozen synthetic judgment label map cannot be represented through
this adapter; they fail explicitly. No new menu, ordinal interpretation,
shortlist, retry or truncation is invented. The model artifact's candidate and
context limits remain enforced.

The original integration was exercised against DMBench 0.2.0 source with
ten pytest tests, including a Hypothesis check that arbitrary public text is
preserved. Its actual evaluator scored a choice result and retained both a
model failure and an unsupported task in the original denominator. Explicit
batch evaluation retained order, grouping and gold isolation across a partial
final chunk. Source
file SHA-256 identities and the tested contract are recorded in the
[integration receipt](../benchmarks/real/dmbench-integration.json).

Twenty additional native-recipe checks use the actual peer role fixtures and
evaluator. They cover text whitespace/Unicode, canonical object/list state,
exact menu order, gold isolation, empty chunks and whole-chunk rejection of
malformed roles. An actual `KaiEncoder` with a character-tokenizer fixture
configured with `max_options=64` and `max_length=512` rejects 65 candidates
and oversized context without loading weights. These checks establish the
configured fixture's validation; they do not establish the released artifact's
candidate-count or token-length limits. The adapter preserves whichever limits
the loaded model declares. The original ten tests still pass. The
separate [native integration receipt](../benchmarks/real/dmbench-native-integration.json)
binds the adapter, peer helper/API/fixtures and tests by hash. This is
interface evidence; no native-recipe model-quality or performance result
has been measured here. Original pilot hashes and results remain unchanged.

An earlier full-model pilot with the default `dmbench-verbatim-choice-v1`
recipe exercised the actual DMBench evaluator through the downloaded full
Kai artifact on MLX GPU, in FP32. It used the first
four fixed training-source BANKING77 development queries, preserving their
choice IDs, descriptions, order and independently supplied labels. Scalar and
two-request batch conditions both answered all four correctly, with no
inference errors. The original assay's separate classification instruction
was omitted because the default recipe forwards public query text verbatim
into an empty context. The
[native pilot receipt](../benchmarks/real/dmbench-native-pilot.json) retains
every prediction, probabilities, actual DMBench timing, model identity and
source/version hashes. This single execution per condition has no warmup or
repetition protocol and supports no speed or broad model-quality claim.

Reproduce the bounded pilot with both projects installed or DMBench on
`PYTHONPATH`:

```sh
PYTHONPATH=/path/to/dmbench/src python -m benchmarks.real.dmbench.pilot \
  /local/kai-bundle
```

Run optional integration checks against an installed DMBench or a source
checkout:

```sh
PYTHONPATH=/path/to/dmbench/src pytest \
  tests/test_dmbench.py tests/interop/dmbench/test_native.py
```

Without DMBench, these optional tests are skipped; a skip is not a verified
integration result.
