files.text:
# Implementation evidence, 2026-10-05

Wyat loads local decision models once, supports native batching and HTTP,
evaluates labeled JSONL, and exposes scalar/batch adapters to DMBench. The eventual
Wyat architecture remains open. Released Kai is a concrete reference contract.

## Verification

The current engine and scientific-tool increments passed **777 pytest tests**,
including Hypothesis, native MLX CPU/Metal checks and all thirty actual DMBench
integration checks, with no skips. One upstream Starlette TestClient deprecation
warning remained. Independent focused checks and source/receipt audits also
passed. Ruff lint/formatting pass; strict mypy passes all 129 current production,
test and maintained experiment Python files. Historical executed-source archives are
preserved byte-for-byte rather than treated as maintained modules.
Optional DMBench types were checked against its real source. Wyat ships `py.typed`.
The [current regression snapshot](../benchmarks/real/engine-attention-observer-verification.json)
retains the outcomes and exact source archive for all 129 maintained files.
The earlier [733-test](../benchmarks/real/engine-attention-verification.json),
[709-test](../benchmarks/real/engine-unroll-cuda-verification.json),
[626-test](../benchmarks/real/mlx-tile-tooling-verification.json),
[568-test](../benchmarks/real/mlx-mixed-tooling-verification.json),
[517-test](../benchmarks/real/cpu-prefix-latency-verification.json),
[482-test](../benchmarks/real/cpu-prefix-memory-verification.json),
[434-test](../benchmarks/real/cpu-prefix-tooling-verification.json)
and [384-test](../benchmarks/real/engine-tooling-verification.json) snapshots
remain unchanged. Formatting also checks six preserved historical Python snapshots.

Wheel and source distribution build successfully. All 20 production Python
files in the wheel match current source bytes; the typed marker and attribution
are included, with no model weights. Isolated core import/CLI help work with
site packages disabled. The earlier
[packaging receipt](../benchmarks/real/package-engine-tooling-verification.json) hashes both
distributions and every production source file. The corrected public MLX loader also completed GPU
scoring in the separate MLX-only environment with Torch absent and unimported.
Source-distribution inspection exposed raw Instruments capture inclusion despite
nested Git ignore rules. Explicit Hatch exclusions now remove trace bundles and
raw XML; distribution inspection checks their absence directly.
The projection experiment retains actual weight/input/output tensors locally.
Git and source-distribution exclusions also remove `*.tensors.safetensors`;
the rebuilt distributions contain no weights. Sanitized receipts remain included.
The preceding distribution identities and capture-exclusion checks remain in
the independently generated [earlier packaging receipt](../benchmarks/real/package-unroll-verification.json).
The observer increment has its separate
[packaging receipt](../benchmarks/real/package-attention-verification.json).
Both verify the production bytes, typed marker and exclusions; packaging does
not establish inference quality or speed. No artifact has been published.

Independent review reproduced activation/tokenizer mismatches and uncaught
corrupt-file errors. The artifact boundary now rejects non-SiLU backbones.
Tokenizer policy delegates to maintained local-only Hugging Face loading with
custom code disabled. Eighteen focused tests cover metadata, Qwen normalization,
spacing, special tokens, custom-code isolation and malformed JSON. Alternate
version-selected tokenizer files are rejected pending a consumed-file contract.
Torch validates tokenization before allocating its backbone; truncated backbone
and head Safetensors failures now become clear loader errors.

Earlier subprocess checks verified JSONL, failure-inclusive evaluation, and a
temporary localhost HTTP server against the offline tiny fixture. The full
suite retains cancellation/admission regressions: client cancellation cannot
admit new inference until the actual worker finishes.

## Real model and data

The pinned Kai release is revision `cd49ea3813fd8ba0928a9a23ef6c9a0f2f0cd764`,
model identity `kai:1f5525e01de43a724c71824579ef5195595fba916ce1e02be7bbbbea50f25cee`.
The [development protocol](real-benchmark.md) fixes 77 independently annotated
BANKING77 training-source queries with deterministic six-choice menus. Prior
model exposure is unknown. This changed task is neither the official 77-way
score nor held-out Wyat quality evidence.

CPU and FP32 MLX retained every full ranking and selected label on all 77 cases;
both scored 67/77. Largest observed runtime drift was `1.29e-5` logits and
`2.46e-6` probability. Full references and repeated raw outputs remain in
[benchmarks/real](../benchmarks/real). Repeating cases does not create additional
independent labeled observations.

The final CPU/MLX comparison uses the public CLI, identical model/requests,
batch eight, cache zero, FP32, eight CPU threads, one warmup and five alternating
pairs. Both initial and post-review measurements are preserved. The
[current receipt](../benchmarks/real/runtime-cpu-mlx77.json) is authoritative for
final-source behavior. Timings exclude loading/HTTP; batch residence excludes
admission queues. Shared process high-water RSS is not per-engine memory.
On the M4 Pro, the final paired median was **2.02x** (5th–95th paired percentiles
1.85x–2.16x); useful throughput was 25.84 requests/s on MLX versus 12.89 on CPU.
The 385 repeated rankings/decisions all agreed; these are 77 unique cases.

## Rejected hypotheses

| Experiment | Observation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CPU causal-only attention | Parity; about 1.02x variable timing | Simpler logic, no meaningful speed claim |
| MLX compilation | Parity; 0.990x median | Eager default |
| CPU Inductor | Parity; 0.919x median, 30.62 s cold JIT/cohort | Experimental only |
| QNNPACK INT8 Linear | About 3x slower; substantial ranking/score drift | Rejected |
| MLX whole-backbone BF16 | Eight rankings changed; probability drift 0.0191 | Rejected |
| MLX whole-backbone FP16 | One ranking changed; probability drift 0.00241 | Rejected |
| MLX packed QKV/gate-up/both | Strict parity; medians 0.984x/0.996x/0.976x | Maintained projections retained |
| MLX exact padding/length grouping | Less configured work; paired variation crosses regression | Inconclusive; no promotion |
| Six CPU thread budgets | Eight best sampled; all 3,234 outputs pass | Eight retained; fitted peak is descriptive |
| [CPU FP32 gate/up packing](analysis/cpu.md) | Strict parity; B8 median 1.02047x, B1 1.01494x | Scalar misses original 1.02 threshold; experimental only |
| [Frozen CPU projection max-autotune](analysis/cpu.md) | Selected ATen `mm` over slower NEON CPP; warm median 0.98404x | One real projection; no complete-engine compile promotion |
| [MLX exact FP16 MLP storage](analysis/precision.md) | All 84 tensors contain changed values; all six fixed arms ineligible | Rejected before inference; exact guard preserved |
| [MLX BF16 MLP-role products](analysis/bfloat.md) | All three arms fail strict logit/probability gates at B8 and B1; top choices unchanged | Completed numerical negative; no timing or promotion |

Tiny random-model receipts remain explicitly synthetic. No 20x real-model or
upstream-service speedup is supported. Numerical gates were not weakened to
accept a candidate.

## Resource optimization

The [inactive-cache experiment](analysis/cache.md) found that a 512 MiB MLX
allocator-cache cap reduces retained active-plus-cache allocation from 9.32 GB
to 2.93 GB at batch eight, with about 0.7% lower throughput. Scalar allocation
fell from 6.82 GB to 2.93 GB with about 1.9% lower throughput. This is allocator
accounting, not per-engine RSS or a hard bound on live weights/activations.
Every observed ranking/selection passed the unchanged score/probability gates.
The explicit process-owned `--mlx-cache-limit-mib` CLI option preserves the
runtime default when omitted. Eighteen CLI tests and a
[pinned-model smoke check](../benchmarks/analysis/results/mlx-cli-cache-smoke.json)
verify its conversion, eligibility, ordering and output behavior.

The [decomposition protocol](analysis/plan.md) connects Amdahl ceilings, raw
scaling sweeps, roofline work estimates, profiler overhead and rejected fits.
The [CPU operator profile](analysis/cpu.md) independently observed flash GQA
in all 28 layers and no repeated K/V expansion. GEMMs accounted for about
75.7% of profiled self time, versus 8.61% for flash attention. All forty sampled
outputs matched the frozen reference exactly; profile fractions remain
diagnostics rather than ordinary latency measurements.
The completed [endpoint assay](analysis/mlx.md) preserved strict parity and
measured 1.024x batch-eight versus 1.019x scalar median speedup. The completed
[prefix assay](analysis/prefix.md) measured 1.078x versus 1.011x, with about
206 MB greater batch-eight peak active allocation. Both scalar confirmations
missed the predeclared 1.02 threshold, so their standalone paths remain
experimental. A separately measured combined implementation passed both gates:
1.107x batch-eight and 1.026x scalar, with all five pairs faster at each shape.
An independent audit verified raw cycles, source archives, sample percentiles
and every CPU-reference ranking/decision. Prefix build cost was about 33 ms,
excluded from warmed timing, and batch-eight peak active allocation rose about
206 MB. The gain applies to this fixed-prefix cohort and cache policy.

The final opt-in production [prefix scorer](analysis/prefix.md) shares native
batch packing and one typed endpoint primitive with the experiments. It builds
one exact immutable token prefix eagerly, requires fixed weights/device/encoder,
rejects compiled or scaled-RoPE bases, and falls back intact when any request
mismatches or overlaps its readouts. Default loading and CLI behavior stay on
full prefill. Actual `Model` and HTTP tests cover matching and fallback calls;
a Torch-free MLX tiny fixture also preserves the full reference.

Final-source five-pair confirmation measured **1.113x at batch eight** and
**1.026x scalar**, with paired sample p05 values 1.108x and 1.020x. Both original
gates pass; all CPU-reference rankings and decisions agree. The separate
[batch-eight receipt](../benchmarks/analysis/results/mlx-prefix-production77-b8.json)
and [scalar receipt](../benchmarks/analysis/results/mlx-prefix-production77-b1.json)
retain every cycle and identical source archives. Prefix setup took
32.63/33.57 ms outside warmed timing. These sample percentiles are not confidence
intervals, and the experiment does not establish online serving gains.

The separate [CPU prefix experiment](analysis/cpu.md) uses maintained Qwen3
masking, RoPE and DynamicCache with the full final block. Native Mac availability
flags permit masked CPU GQA in the installed Transformers/Torch combination;
the first-eight profiler directly confirmed flash attention and unexpanded K/V.
Its two ordinary controls remained descriptive before full confirmation.
Five alternating pairs then measured **1.101x batch-eight** and **1.076x scalar**
median speedup. Both shapes passed the prospectively strengthened four-condition
CPU policy: median >=1.02, paired p05 >1, greater aggregate throughput and no
cohort p95 regression. All 2,156 screen/warm/measured outputs preserved complete
CPU-reference rankings and selections; maximum logit/probability drift was
`9.954e-6`/`1.560e-6`. Each cycle retained 67/77 correct on the same development
cases. The [independent combined audit](../benchmarks/analysis/results/torch-prefix77-review.json)
retains receipt, journal, executed-source, input and reference identities.
Cold prefix setup took 69.01/67.70 ms outside timing; fresh per-call cache copying
remained inside. This supports a CPU production candidate for the measured
fixed-prefix cohort; CPU production code has not changed.

The maintained cache retains suffix K/V through each invocation. A separate
[one-use lifecycle proof](../benchmarks/analysis/results/torch-prefix-lifetime-feasibility.json)
passed eight tiny tests and an independent rerun, covering ordered updates,
storage lifetime, offset masks and full hidden-state parity. Its first observer
failure is retained. Releasing references supported the subsequent resource
experiment; the lifecycle proof itself established no physical RSS or speed
savings. Calculated logical tensor bytes
and shared cumulative process high-water RSS are distinct observations.

The subsequent [six-process resource screen](../benchmarks/analysis/results/torch-prefix-memory-review.json)
used three fresh serial alternating arm pairs on the frozen first eight cases.
All 288 raw outputs preserved the CPU-reference ranking and numerical gates;
each process directly confirmed masked flash GQA and complete layer inventories.
Observed selected storage capacity, including fixed prefix snapshots and current
returned K/V, fell from 358,055,936 to 62,554,112 bytes. This excludes transient
projection inputs, concatenation overlaps, activations and allocator overhead.
Separately sampled inference-body RSS fell by **421–428 MB (9.53–9.67%)**;
each pair passed the prospectively declared 64 MiB-or-5% effect screen. All
samples met the declared interior-count and conservative coverage-gap gates.
Observer cycles took 1.484–1.541x ordinary duration, and post-profile RSS could
exceed the sampled body peak. The evidence supports this specific body-sampled
process resource behavior, with eight unique development cases. It establishes
neither an unobserved whole-run peak nor a speed or held-out quality gain.

The subsequent observer-free full77 latency experiment completed four fresh
serial processes, with one warmup and five alternating measured pairs per
comparison. Its [independent raw audit](../benchmarks/analysis/results/torch-one-use-latency-review.json)
reconstructs all outcomes, source identities, walls and prospective gates.
Every returned warmup and measured outcome faced the frozen CPU
reference: all **3,696 checks** passed, with 67/77 correct per cycle. These remain
77 unique development cases. Cold prefix construction stayed outside timing;
fresh per-call cache copies remained inside. The original full-prefill scorer
and the common retained-prefix path were distinct controls.

| One-use candidate versus control | Batch | Median ratio | Paired p05 | Cohort p95 ratio | Prospective performance result |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Retained prefix | 8 | 0.99979 | 0.99688 | 1.00128 | Fail |
| Retained prefix | 1 | 1.00143 | 0.99875 | 0.98884 | Fail |
| Original full prefill | 8 | 1.10928 | 1.08829 | 0.91822 | Pass |
| Original full prefill | 1 | 1.07313 | 1.05803 | 0.94289 | Pass |

Both comparisons require paired p05 >1, aggregate throughput >1 and no cohort
p95 regression; the median threshold is >=1 for retained-owner selection and
the unchanged >=1.02 for full-prefill improvement. The retained comparisons
failed their declared gates despite ratios close to parity. Full-prefill gains
support prefix reuse on this workload; they do not override those negatives.
No timeout occurred under the four owned 180-second caps; all groups were reaped.
The runner preserves raw returned cycles before validation and rejects missing
cycles, wrong identities and warmup-only drift. Internal partial cycles remain
unknown if canonical `benchmark_pair` never returns. One-use selection is
unsupported under the declared policy; CPU production code and defaults remain
unchanged. Future retained-prefix integration remains a separate decision.
The resource and latency gains are not multiplied or pooled.

The [bounded MLX mixed-weight projection experiment](analysis/mixed.md) completed
with real first-layer gate inputs from those eight cases. Separate actual prefix
and full-prefill captures used batch eight and the declared 192-token scalar
case; all 18 full-model decision checks preserved the CPU reference. The model
and cache owners were released before primitive timing, and weights decoded
from BF16 to their original FP32 bits exactly.

The fixed 32×32×32 custom Metal tile used float SIMD products/accumulation and
local BF16 weight decoding. Both custom storage arms matched maintained FP32
matmul bitwise across all four cold projection shapes: 19,851,264 comparison
elements, zero observed error. All 12 warm and 720 timed outputs reproduced their
admitted cold hashes. The [independent audit](../benchmarks/analysis/results/mlx-mixed-gate-review.json)
also checked 256 scalar FP64 dots, with largest absolute error `3.917e-6`.

| Projection shape | Mixed / maintained paired median speed ratio | Paired p05 | Prospective result |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Prefix scalar, M=167 | 0.54590 | 0.50923 | Fail |
| Prefix batch eight, M=1336 | 0.40104 | 0.38013 | Fail |
| Full scalar, M=192 | 0.49630 | 0.47184 | Fail |
| Full batch eight, M=1536 | 0.35713 | 0.34930 | Fail |

Ratios are maintained time divided by mixed time; values below one mean slower.
All six order permutations and ten synchronized dispatches per arm/block remain
recorded. Outside-interval output hashing separates dispatches and can perturb
execution, so these are conditional primitive timings, not unobserved throughput.
The owned child completed in 9.816 seconds under its 180-second cap, restored the
allocator-cache cap and was reaped. Raw inputs/cold outputs remain ignored tensor
artifacts. No custom primitive was promoted and no end-to-end speed gain follows.

Both custom FP32 and BF16 storage arms were slow. The
[source-level tile account](analysis/mixed-tile.md) motivated the separately
declared [64×64 output-reuse trial](analysis/tile.md). It reused the exact
captured activations and weights, without recapturing a model. Maintained and
frozen32 cold bits reproduced their previous outputs; both new64 storage arms
also matched maintained FP32 exactly at all four shapes. All 12 warm and 720
timed outputs reproduced their respective cold hashes.

| Projection shape | Maintained / new64 paired median | Paired p05 | Frozen32 / new64 paired median |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Prefix scalar, M=167 | 0.18167 | 0.17653 | 0.37292 |
| Prefix batch eight, M=1336 | 0.14830 | 0.14566 | 0.36384 |
| Full scalar, M=192 | 0.19830 | 0.17211 | 0.38894 |
| Full batch eight, M=1536 | 0.14271 | 0.14020 | 0.39482 |

The unchanged maintained comparison fails at both required prefix shapes;
full-shape controls also fail. The larger tile is slower than the live frozen32
control. Lower logical read counts therefore did not improve this implementation.
The [real receipt](../benchmarks/analysis/results/mlx-tile64-gate.json) retains
every permutation and raw dispatch. The owned child was terminal after 9.465
seconds without timeout, restored the allocator-cache limit and was reaped.
The [independent CPU-only audit](../benchmarks/analysis/results/mlx-tile64-gate-review.json)
verified all 123 current trial sources, historical identities, 16 cold arrays,
732 warm/timed hashes and every paired ratio. All 29,776,896 candidate/reference
comparison elements had zero error. Its 256 scalar FP64 dot anchors passed with
maximum absolute error `3.698e-6`. The prospective declaration remains unchanged.
Production bytes and prior experiments remain unchanged. No kernel was selected.
Register spills, occupancy and shared-memory stalls remain possible explanations,
not observed causes. Output hashing has the same observer limitation as the
initial trial; no whole-engine speed claim follows. The
[next diagnostic](analysis/tile-next.md) identified public capture/compiler
interfaces and a separately testable fragment-loop unrolling hypothesis.

The [explicit fragment-loop unrolling trial](analysis/unroll.md) changed only
seven static-loop directives. All 16 cold arrays and 732 warm/timed hashes still
matched maintained FP32 exactly. Its paired medians improved over frozen64 by
1.927x scalar and 1.995x batch eight at the prefix shapes, but the required
maintained/unrolled ratios were only 0.35280x and 0.29556x (p05 0.33534x and
0.29292x). Both full-shape controls also failed. This improves the prototype and
rejects promotion against the maintained implementation. The
[raw receipt](../benchmarks/analysis/results/mlx-unroll64-gate.json) preserves
every order and dispatch; its owned worker completed in 9.819 seconds without
timeout and restored its cache policy. The
[independent audit](../benchmarks/analysis/results/mlx-unroll64-gate-review.json)
verified 131 consumed sources, all outputs and ratios, and 256 FP64 anchors.
No register-spill or whole-engine speed claim follows.

The [bounded Metal diagnostic](analysis/trace.md) captured one ready batch-eight
dispatch for each frozen32/frozen64 kernel. The
[successful capture receipt](../benchmarks/analysis/results/mlx-ready-capture2.json)
retains output hashes and raw bundle inventories. An earlier inventory check
rejected an internal buffer alias; that incomplete receipt remains intact.
The corrected guard admits only aliases resolving to contained regular files.
The offline Metal compiler was unavailable; one owned headless replay attempt
returned no profiling fields before its 120-second cap. Its client was killed
and reaped, with no matching process in the final snapshot; hidden XPC session
state remains unknown. The
[diagnostic audit](../benchmarks/analysis/results/mlx-ready-capture-review.json)
preserves this failure and verifies the original captures stayed unchanged.
Spills, occupancy and shared-memory stalls remain unmeasured.

## Coordination and limits

DMBench owns benchmark contracts, provenance, grouping and metrics; Wyat owns
inference and deployment. Both projects independently tested the single Wyat
translation helper. A [four-case native pilot](../benchmarks/real/dmbench-native-pilot.json)
ran actual scalar/batch DMBench evaluation through FP32 MLX without errors and
with identical answers. Its empty-context, verbatim-text recipe is explicit.
Single-run pilot timing supports no speed comparison.
The optional `dmbench-native-choice-v1` recipe now uses DMBench's actual role
validator and canonical serializer, preserving supplied choices and separating
instructions from state. Its [integration receipt](../benchmarks/real/dmbench-native-integration.json)
hashes peer and Wyat sources and two real peer fixtures. It establishes adapter
mechanics, not native-recipe model quality or throughput; the old pilot used
`dmbench-verbatim-choice-v1`. Both recipes retain whole-chunk preflight and
encoder limits without truncation or menu reduction.
The separately frozen [30-case native development assay](../benchmarks/real/dmbench-native-dev-assay.json)
completed scalar and batch-six evaluation with all cases retained. Six full
CLINC menus exceeded the declared 2,048-token setting; all 24 authored cases
were admitted, with identical selections and maximum probability drift
`6.27e-8`. Independent raw-output inspection also retained all 24 full rankings
and finite normalized distributions. The released artifact permits 255 choices;
the 64-choice boundary belongs to a configured test fixture. Accuracy was
4/30 including failures in both reports. That modest development observation
must not be confused with passing interoperability checks or representative
model quality. Prior exposure is unknown; no test split or reserved Wyat
confirmation cohort was used.

Earlier RTX 4070 Ti probes sampled 71–99% utilization. A
[fresh observer-timestamped snapshot](../benchmarks/analysis/results/cuda-availability-20261005T062156Z.json)
found zero utilization and 128 MiB allocated. These observations are not a
reservation. Canonical model assets were transferred to an owned private
experiment directory; existing environments remain unchanged. The
[prospective CUDA control](analysis/cuda-run.md) requires exact asset/runtime
admission and uncontended pre-allocation and per-batch observations.
The [real batch-one FP32 cohort](../benchmarks/analysis/results/cuda-fp32-b1.json)
preserved all 77 selections and full rankings, with 67/77 labeled correct and
no failures. Maximum logit drift was `1.723e-5`; probability drift was `2.821e-6`.
All 231 observed projection/head events had FP32 inputs/outputs and disabled
autocast; math SDPA was forced. The parent completed in 11.184 seconds without
timeout; peak allocated/reserved memory was 2.417/2.441 GB. These are cold,
observer-instrumented numerical controls, not speed benchmarks.
The [independent raw audit](../benchmarks/analysis/results/cuda-fp32-b1-review.json)
verified every row, all 44 assets and 33 consumed sources, package/build pins,
parent cleanup and the terminal 128 MiB/zero-utilization/no-compute-owner
snapshot. One independently reconstructed probability differed by one ULP
across hosts; the audit retains its initial exact-serialization failure and
uses a two-ULP derived-softmax check. The original `1e-4` probability gate and
all ranking/logit gates remain unchanged; the precise cause was not established.
The separately run [batch-eight FP32 control](../benchmarks/analysis/results/cuda-fp32-b8.json)
also preserved every selection and full ranking against both CPU and CUDA
batch one. Maximum CPU logit/probability drift was `1.395e-5`/`2.566e-6`;
peak allocated/reserved memory was 2.532/2.691 GB. Its parent completed in
8.580 seconds without timeout. Batch geometry passed this numerical assay;
this cold diagnostic cannot compare speed with batch one. Its
[independent raw audit](../benchmarks/analysis/results/cuda-fp32-b8-review.json)
verified all rows, ten batches, 30 dtype events and immutable control identities.

The [released CUDA BF16 recipe](../benchmarks/analysis/results/cuda-released-b1.json)
returned all 77 finite predictions with the expected observed projection/head
dtypes and unchanged top choices and 67 correct labels. Only 72/77 full ranks
matched CPU; maximum logit/probability drift was `0.077878`/`0.015278`.
The same strict gates also failed against CUDA FP32 batch one. Peak
allocated/reserved memory was 1.529/1.539 GB. Its parent was terminal in
12.593 seconds with exit one and no timeout: a completed negative quality
result, not an omitted failure. The recipe changes arithmetic and attention
selection together; this assay does not isolate a particular cause of drift.
The [independent negative-result audit](../benchmarks/analysis/results/cuda-released-b1-review.json)
confirmed the five changed ranks: `banking77-train-01221`, `-07093`, `-01726`,
`-06546` and `-08199`. All 77 case-level logit gates and 66 probability gates
failed against CPU. No BF16 batch-eight trial, retry or production precision
change followed.
The [final release snapshot](../benchmarks/analysis/results/cuda-final-release-20261005.json)
retains per-command statuses: 128 MiB allocated, zero utilization, no compute
owner and no matching owned runner after all three children exited.
CUDA performance and production promotion remain unestablished.
Production traffic, reserved confirmation, authentication/TLS and the eventual
Wyat export contract also remain outside this evidence. Necessary decisions are
in [open-question.md](../open-question.md).

Kai code is separated into `backends/kai/artifact.py`, `encoding.py`, `torch.py`
and `mlx.py`; loading lives in `loading/local.py`. Experiment runners are grouped by device/task with short names;
package initializers contain no inference logic. Historical receipt bytes stay
unchanged. The original source-hashed pilot is archived as text when its
runnable reproducer moves.

## CUDA efficient-attention experiment preparation

The [prospective first-eight screen](analysis/attention.md) uses the maintained
Transformers causal-mask path to repeat KV heads before PyTorch efficient
attention. Its FP32 tensor interface does not establish IEEE internal arithmetic;
the declared FastF32 candidate must pass the original numerical and full-ranking
gates. Twenty-four focused CPU/fake checks cover causal equivalence, mask
construction, context restoration, source admission, partial failures and final
receipt failures. Independent review passed before GPU release. The full
733-test preparation regression preserves all twenty production sources.
Native execution and actual dispatch require separately recorded observations;
local tests alone support no complete inference speed claim.

The [initial real batch-one screen](../benchmarks/analysis/results/cuda-attention-b1.json)
retains eighteen ordinary/profile outcomes on eight unique development cases.
Both ordinary arms preserve all eight choices/full rankings and seven correct
labels. The efficient arm's largest CPU-reference logit/probability differences
are `1.2040e-5`/`1.3444e-6`. An
[independent raw audit](../benchmarks/analysis/results/cuda-attention-b1-review.json)
verified these unchanged gates and individual terminal release queries.
The original dispatch flag remains false and the 9.63-second parent exits 1:
the public observer did not expose the internal operator schema expected by
its gate. Separate profiler observations contain twenty-eight private efficient
operators and twenty-eight FP32 CUTLASS attention kernels. Additive-bias strides
remain unobserved. These diagnostic observations establish neither ordinary
latency nor full77/held-out quality, and do not override the original failed flag.
A separately declared observation correction will test that boundary directly.

The observer correction passes sixty-eight focused tests and the complete
777-test native regression. Independent AST comparison preserves all fourteen
original non-observer test functions. New checks challenge missing private/kernel
observations, fallback operators, extra FP16 kernels, positional/keyword flags,
Boolean/integer aliases and explicit/nonfinite scales. Source inspection and a
local frozen-HF CPU call establish that Qwen supplies the mathematical scale
`128**-0.5` explicitly; this local Torch version does not establish the remote
binary's dispatch. The corrected diagnostic requires both public metadata and
private profiler/kernel evidence. The
[independent preparation audit](../benchmarks/analysis/results/cuda-attention-observer-local-review.json)
checks all 129 current sources, the three approved Python differences, all
twenty production files, original histories and the seven-file v2 declaration.
Its native rerun remains separately gated.

The [corrected batch-one screen](../benchmarks/analysis/results/cuda-attention-observer-b1.json)
passes quality and dispatch with the separate v2 source identity; its
[independent raw audit](../benchmarks/analysis/results/cuda-attention-observer-b1-review.json)
rebuilds all eighteen outcomes and verifies both observation boundaries.
The remote public call records the explicit scale `0.08838834764831845`.
Twenty-eight private efficient/forward operators and twenty-eight FP32 SM80
CUTLASS kernels execute without observed fallback. The selector cannot represent
that explicit scale; converted-bias strides and precise internal arithmetic stay
unknown. The parent exits zero in 9.58 seconds under its 180-second cap, and
individually attributed queries verify idle GPU and no owned runner. Release
observation UTC was not captured in this sidecar and remains unknown. The
initial negative flags and original archived bytes are unchanged. These repeats
cover the same eight development cases, not additional independent quality data;
loading, occupancy queries and intrusive profiling preclude a speed claim.

The [corrected batch-eight screen](../benchmarks/analysis/results/cuda-attention-observer-b8.json)
and its [independent raw audit](../benchmarks/analysis/results/cuda-attention-observer-b8-review.json)
retain all thirty-two ordinary/profile outcomes over the same eight cases, with
zero failures and unchanged choices/full rankings. Both ordinary arms score
seven correct. Largest candidate CPU-reference logit/probability differences
are `1.1861e-5`/`1.0655e-6`; CUDA-control differences are `9.8944e-6`/`1.3008e-6`.
Public Q/K/V are `[8,16,192,128]` FP32; the Boolean mask is `[1,1,192,192]`.
Twenty-eight private efficient/forward events and twenty-eight FP32 attention
kernels pass the corrected gate without observed fallback. The 9.13-second
parent exits zero; timestamped individual release queries at
`2026-10-05T08:33:01Z` confirm idle GPU and no owned runner. All current sources
and original controls remain exact. Neither job accepts a performance result
or changes production. Full77 confirmation and warmed alternating comparisons
remain necessary before proposing this candidate for deployment.

# Native MLX inference

Wyat uses [MLX-LM's Qwen3 backbone](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm/blob/v0.31.3/mlx_lm/models/qwen3.py)
for Apple Silicon. The runtime reads a local full Kai choice checkpoint directly;
there is no model conversion, downloaded Python execution, vocabulary projection,
generation loop, or persistent KV cache in the default scorer. The eventual Wyat architecture remains
open; this backend implements the currently released Kai contract.

```python
from wyat import Candidate, Model, Request
from wyat.backends.kai.mlx import MLXKaiScorer

scorer = MLXKaiScorer.from_directory("/models/kai", device="gpu")
model = Model(scorer, scorer.model_id)
request = Request(
    query="Where should this request go?",
    context="I need to reset my password.",
    candidates=(Candidate("account", "Account access"), Candidate("sales", "Sales")),
)
decision = model.decide(request)
```

`device="cpu"` is available for runtime parity checks. On macOS, even importing
the Metal-enabled MLX wheel requires access to the Metal device; a sandbox that
hides it cannot establish a passing inference check.

The loader shares artifact validation, file hashes and segmented tokenization
with the Torch backend. It rejects missing, unexpected, malformed and nonfinite
weights. Backbone tensors are expanded losslessly from BF16 storage to FP32;
the decision head stays FP32, including its exact GELU and LayerNorm with
epsilon `1e-5`. No quantization or reduced-precision approximation is enabled.

For each batch, the backbone runs one causal prefill. Candidate endpoints and
the final query endpoint are gathered before head scoring. Rows are right-padded;
the causal mask excludes all future padding from each selected endpoint. Output
rows retain the original request and candidate order. `score_many` evaluates the
MLX graph and materializes host floats before returning, so wall-clock timings
include device execution.

`compile=True` opts into [MLX compilation](https://ml-explore.github.io/mlx/build/html/usage/compile.html).
Weights are loaded once and captured as immutable inference parameters. Measure
cold compilation separately from warm throughput: compiled graphs specialize
to input shapes and a new batch shape can incur compilation. It remains opt-in
until the selected real workload demonstrates a benefit within its parity gate.

Applications sharing an exact fixed token prefix can explicitly construct an
eager `PrefixScorer` around an uncompiled native base. It retains immutable
prefix K/V state, uses fresh suffix cache owners and falls back whole batches on
mismatches. [Prefix usage and its measured limits](analysis/prefix.md) describe
the resource contract. Existing loading and CLI defaults retain full prefill.

MLX-LM depends on Transformers and can initialize its optional Torch integration
when Torch happens to be installed. Wyat uses MLX tensors and the maintained Transformers tokenizer policy.
An MLX-only environment needs no Torch installation. A
mixed environment may still import Torch through upstream package initialization;
this is an upstream optional import rather than an inference requirement.
The clean installation `uv pip install -e '.[mlx]'` was checked in a separate
environment on 2026-10-05: a tiny local checkpoint completed GPU scoring with
both `importlib.util.find_spec("torch") is None` and `"torch" not in sys.modules`.
That environment used MLX 0.32.3, MLX-LM 0.31.3 and Transformers 5.17.0.

The checks in `tests/backends/kai/test_mlx.py` compare native head arithmetic and complete
tiny checkpoint inference against Torch, exercise Unicode serialization,
variable-length batches, compilation and missing weights, and load a checkpoint
in a fresh process. Tiny random weights establish
mechanics only. Real-data accuracy, numerical drift and hardware performance must
be established through the recorded full-checkpoint benchmark.

The real FP32 Metal run on 2026-10-05 used 77 frozen BANKING77 development
requests with six supplied candidates, retaining all 77 Torch reference rankings
and decisions. The largest logit difference was `1.29e-5`; the largest probability
difference was `2.46e-6`. Both runtimes selected the expected label in 67 of 77
cases. This measures inference preservation on that cohort; the checkpoint's
exposure to BANKING77 is unknown.

Five paired full-cohort runs measured a median compiled/eager speedup of `0.990x`
(5th–95th paired percentiles: `0.950x`–`1.080x`). Compilation preserved the
quality gate but did not support a throughput improvement. The eager default is
retained. Raw observations and the reproducer live in
`benchmarks/real/mlx-fp32-parity77.json`, `mlx-fp32-compile77.json` and
`benchmarks/real/mlx/fp32.py`.

A separate BF16-backbone hypothesis retained all selected labels but changed
eight complete rankings. Maximum drift reached `0.108` logits and `0.0191`
probability, exceeding the declared `1e-3` logit and `1e-4` probability gates.
It was rejected; no production precision flag was added. Its raw outcomes and
reproducer remain in `mlx-bf16-screen77.json` and `benchmarks/real/mlx/precision.py`.

FP16 was tested separately because it retains more mantissa precision than
BF16. All converted parameters and outputs were finite; selected labels and
accuracy stayed unchanged. One full ranking changed, with maximum drift of
`0.0137` logits and `0.00241` probability, so it also failed the same gate.
No production dtype flag was added. Reproduce `mlx-fp16-screen77.json` with
`python benchmarks/real/mlx/precision.py --dtype float16`; the same runner handles
both precision experiments without a second inference implementation.

files.text:
# Measuring an engine change

Use the same local model artifact and labeled request cohort for both engines.
Freeze the candidate configuration and quality tolerances before inference.
Change one setting at a time: batching, token caching, attention implementation,
precision, device or runtime. Keep the baseline description precise; a speedup
over singleton Wyat is not a speedup over the upstream server.

The public `wyat benchmark` command accepts cases on stdin and emits the complete
JSON receipt on stdout; see the [CLI example](../README.md#measure-an-engine-change).
The final [CPU/MLX receipt](../benchmarks/real/runtime-cpu-mlx77.json) uses the
entire 77-case cohort, batch eight, cache zero and eight CPU threads. Its paired
median is 2.02x, with 1.85x–2.16x paired 5th–95th percentiles. All rankings and
decisions agree. This compares FP32 CPU and Metal runtimes on the M4 Pro;
the repeated ratios are measurement variation, not confidence intervals.

```python
import json
from pathlib import Path

import wyat
from wyat.benchmark import BenchmarkEngine, BenchmarkProtocol, benchmark_pair
from wyat.evaluation import case_from_dict

path = Path("benchmarks/real/banking77-train-dev-menu6.jsonl")
cases = tuple(case_from_dict(json.loads(line)) for line in path.read_text().splitlines())
model = wyat.load("/local/kai-bundle", device="cpu")
report = benchmark_pair(
    BenchmarkEngine("singleton", model, batch_size=1,
                    conditions={"device": "cpu", "optimization": "none"}),
    BenchmarkEngine("batch4", model, batch_size=4,
                    conditions={"device": "cpu", "optimization": "batching"}),
    cases[:16],
    protocol=BenchmarkProtocol(repeats=5, warmup=1),
)
Path("measurement.json").write_text(
    json.dumps(report.to_dict(), indent=2, allow_nan=False) + "\n"
)
```

The example compares batch scheduling on the same loaded model. Separate loaded
engines are needed to compare distinct runtime options. Running independently
loaded models in one process shares host and device memory: process RSS is not
per-engine memory usage. For a deployable memory comparison, run each arm in an
isolated process and record loading, idle resident memory and peak memory with
the same model and cohort. OS high-water RSS is cumulative; subtracting two
high-water readings does not measure allocated model memory.

## Predeclared development protocol

The first bounded full-checkpoint assay uses the first 16 cases of the committed
77-row cohort. Its choice is made from case order, before predictions. Each
arm receives every case in the same order, and the canonical input hash binds
IDs, queries, contexts, candidates, task and expected labels. The full cohort
is available for broader development runs. Any subset has its own hash and IDs;
its performance and accuracy cannot be reported as covering all 77 intents.

One complete warmup cohort is excluded from timing statistics; its failures
remain in the receipt and prevent acceptance. At least three measured repetitions
alternate baseline/candidate and candidate/baseline order. Use five or more
repetitions for retained results. Run engines serially, close unrelated heavy
workloads, and record hardware, model identity, software versions, precision,
attention mode, cache size and CPU threads in `conditions`. Repetition intervals
describe measurement variability; they do not quantify population accuracy or
remove thermal, shared-process or cache-state effects.

Native Torch and MLX scorers materialize host floats before returning. An engine
with deferred work must supply `BenchmarkEngine.synchronize`, called before
each cycle and after each batch. Wall-clock cycles include request packing,
tokenization, model execution, decision interpretation and result bookkeeping.
Loading, warmups, HTTP and JSON encoding are excluded. This is an offline engine
assay; HTTP admission, contention and streaming need separate load tests.

Cycle p50/p95 cover the whole declared cohort. Attempted and successful request
throughputs are separate, so failed requests cannot appear as useful work.
Batch residence latency assigns the full synchronous batch time to each member;
it is not per-request isolated service time, queue latency or throughput divided
by batch size. Every measured repetition retains predictions, logits,
probabilities, rankings, labels, timings and exceptions in original case order.
A failed batch retains each member as a failed prediction.

Default numerical gates are declared before execution: each corresponding logit
must satisfy absolute tolerance `1e-3` or relative tolerance `1e-3`, and every
probability must differ by at most `1e-4`. Every predicted top choice and full
ranking must agree, every request must succeed, and labeled accuracy must not
decrease. Exact ties follow caller order. A near-tie flip still fails selection
agreement even when its numerical differences pass. Repetitions repeat the
same labeled examples; they are not additional independent observations.

A faster candidate with a failed quality gate is rejected. Any precision-specific
relaxed tolerance belongs to a new protocol declared before running; it cannot
be chosen after observing drift simply to make that candidate pass. A passed
parity gate preserves the baseline's measured behavior; it does not establish
that the baseline model is useful. Record labeled accuracy separately.

`speed.median_speedup_positive` reports only whether the paired median exceeds
one. It is separate from the quality `passed` flag and does not establish a
supported performance improvement. Read the complete paired variation, total
successful throughput and p95 latency together before adopting a change. A
near-unit median gain with slower overall throughput or worse tail latency
does not justify a performance claim.

## Source and scope

The committed assay uses actual annotated queries from the official
[PolyAI BANKING77 source](https://github.com/PolyAI-LDN/task-specific-datasets/tree/57ec275d8078af65b7731c2a98be812d844a6d6b/banking_data)
at revision `57ec275d8078af65b7731c2a98be812d844a6d6b`. Only `train.csv`
was downloaded. Its SHA-256 is
`b06e26ac675513959a63135f11b94ea7786ed02da65db93a5650d8838cbc664b`.
Neither the official test split nor reserved Kayak confirmation data is read.

There is one deterministic unique normalized utterance per intent. Six-choice
menus contain the original labeled intent and five deterministic sampled
negatives, with deterministic positive placement. Candidate descriptions
replace underscores in the original intent name with spaces. This is a
changed task and a runtime development assay, **not the official 77-way
BANKING77 score**. Labels come from the dataset rather than from Kai or an LLM.
Source label errors and prior checkpoint exposure remain unknown.

The [dataset manifest](../benchmarks/real/banking77-train-dev-menu6.manifest.json)
records source row IDs, text hashes, normalized utterance groups, label identity,
positive position and the generated byte hash. The source is licensed
[CC-BY-4.0](../benchmarks/real/BANKING77-LICENSE). Attribution: PolyAI;
Casanueva et al. (2020),
[Efficient Intent Detection with Dual Sentence Encoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.04807).

Reproduce from the downloaded pinned training CSV:

```sh
python -m benchmarks.prepare_banking77 /path/to/train.csv
```

An optional `--menu-size 77` generates the corresponding full-intent menus.
An artifact's declared candidate limit may reject those menus; do not increase
that limit simply to run this assay. Any compatible workload needs its own
token-length and resource receipt; it does not become a held-out official score
by using all 77 labels.

files.text:
# Semantic Router Decision 2.0 inference investigation

Inspected on 2026-10-05. Wyat's eventual model shape remains open. This document
describes the released Kai candidate head as one concrete, reversible inference
adapter; it does not make that architecture the contract for every Wyat model.

## Source and evidence

The relevant project is [vLLM Semantic Router](https://github.com/vllm-project/semantic-router),
whose [Decision-2.0-Kai-0.6B release](https://huggingface.co/vllm-sr/Decision-2.0-Kai-0.6B/tree/cd49ea3813fd8ba0928a9a23ef6c9a0f2f0cd764)
includes its inference implementation. It is distinct from Aurelio's package
also named semantic-router. The Hugging Face tree and
[release commit](https://huggingface.co/vllm-sr/Decision-2.0-Kai-0.6B/commit/cd49ea3813fd8ba0928a9a23ef6c9a0f2f0cd764)
were checked through the browser. Local source bytes were inspected from Kayak's
existing release-inspection directory and checked against their stored receipt
and the packaged manifest. The pin is
`cd49ea3813fd8ba0928a9a23ef6c9a0f2f0cd764`, whose builder source commit is
`1b977b6af46e3794859f84468c7366f504f2ec32` and runtime source commit is
`fbedfded8ce33c7c25a99b8fb1f71f733b2c2c44`.

The release gives the runtime, head, weights and tokenizer Apache-2.0 licenses.
Wyat's adapted mathematical implementation retains attribution in `NOTICE`.
The inspected source entry points are:

| File, relative to the pinned release | Observed responsibility | SHA-256 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `decision2/_vendor/dev2model/decision_model.py` | Serialization, segmented tokenization, endpoint gather, head | `1ab1e49bccc8b84632a32565ce666a6db94298372ee891dee5b68e54f80957fb` |
| `decision2/_vendor/dev2model/infer.py` | API validation, stable softmax, response semantics | `7bb9f3cc88f04cd6e4ded62e69f41dd1c7a3d0154a76acdf44c0d73e4163ef58` |
| `decision2/qwen.py` | Local checkpoint loading, precision, per-question batching | `62df8de050d38cd92dc68c12de7d9b65d041a14317feda02ff8ddafc3c69c779` |
| `decision2/fast.py` | ROCm graphs, cast reuse, fused-kernel gates | `d125a98848089ad8be04ef1c799c1daee5ea7704e138c17a874692321a206b54` |
| `decision2/shared_ctx.py` | Opt-in shared-prefix cache and packed attention | `3ea492989258d460b28a5b568e388696a8d07c0b985f960e38d3c99d68620be9` |

## Observed input-to-output path

`state + question + ordered criteria → strict validation → segmented tokens →
causal Qwen3Model → candidate endpoints + final query → FP32 candidate head →
optional Score offsets → temperature + softmax → typed answer`.

Each question is its own row. The prefix renders `Context`, `Task type`,
`Question` and `Options`. Each option is compact, sorted-key JSON containing
`key` and `description`, enclosed by `<option>` tags. Unicode is retained.
Prefix, each entire option and final decision cue are tokenized separately with
no added special tokens. Encoding the visually identical whole string can yield
different tokens at segment boundaries. The candidate representation is the last
token of its complete option, including its closing tag. The query representation
is the final token of the decision cue. Overlength inputs are rejected; no
candidate or context is silently truncated. Rows use right padding to a multiple
of eight; candidate order is preserved. The released prompt allows 2–255 choice
candidates and caps the total encoded input at 8,192 tokens.

The backbone is a causal Qwen3 text model, without vocabulary logits or text
generation. Earlier option endpoints cannot see later options, while the final
query sees all options. Independently cached candidate hidden states therefore
would change this model. Permuting candidates also changes the model input.

For candidate vectors `C[B,N,H]` and query `q[B,H]`, two LayerNorms first compute
`c` and `g`. The shared head computes
`sum(key(c) * query(g), -1) / sqrt(D)` plus
`scalar(GELU(candidate_mlp(c) + query_mlp(g)))`, with `D=256` in the release.
The head disables autocast and calculates in FP32. Invalid padded candidates
are masked. A request's questions run together, subject to a padded-token budget
on the hybrid Qwen3.5 family; this particular Qwen3 model has no such upstream
gated-delta budget.

CPU uses FP32. GPU uses BF16 autocast for the backbone, retaining FP32 residuals,
embeddings, norms and head. Only Linear weights exactly representable as BF16
are stored in BF16. Casting the entire model to BF16 is a different policy.
The release uses SDPA. Its CPU and GPU policies are not claimed numerically equal.

The upstream product response applies a stable host softmax. Choice ties resolve
by original caller order. Confidence is normalized entropy, not accuracy.
Score has model-bound, level-count-specific logit offsets; Noul returns the
probability of the `true` key. Wyat's initial Kai adapter accepts choice only so
the other response semantics cannot be accidentally substituted.

## Optimization hypotheses and their falsifiers

| Hypothesis | Necessary check before accepting it |
| --- | --- |
| Reuse exact option token IDs for repeated menus to reduce host tokenization. | Identical complete IDs and endpoint positions with cache off/on across Unicode, tag-like text, and candidate orders; bounded cache; measure host and complete-request time separately. |
| Batch similar lengths to reduce padding. | Same order restored; batch/singleton decision and probability drift measured, including near ties; serving queue latency counted. |
| Keep BF16-exact Linear weights resident on GPUs to avoid repeated casts. | Exact representability check per parameter; FP32 head/norms remain; compare logits against the existing GPU policy. Upstream already does this. |
| Graph replay/fused elementwise kernels reduce launch overhead on short requests. | Hardware/version gate, exact padded shapes/masks, eager fallback, bounded memory, forced kernel failure, full parity and realistic latency. Upstream already implements this on ROCm. |
| Shared state prefill saves repeated backbone work for multi-question requests. | Isolation between suffixes, original rotary positions, near-tie errors and calibration measured, cache ownership explicit. This changes floating-point order and is not exact by construction. |

The fast path is gated to ROCm and Transformers 5.17; fused kernels are further
gated to gfx942. The graph cache stops admitting shapes after 512 graphs or 4 GiB
of retained outputs and does not evict live captures because upstream observed
GPU faults. Shared context is disabled by default; both tree packing and KV cache
mode can change logits. Upstream explicitly notes that even the normal path is
not strictly batch-invariant.

## Supported conclusions and remaining unknowns

Source inspection supports the data flow and identifies useful controlled
experiments. It does not establish deployed production behavior, reproduce the
released accuracy, or validate upstream performance claims. The original source investigation preceded full-model measurements. Subsequent
released-weight CPU/MLX observations are recorded in the
[implementation receipt](implementation-evidence.md). Tiny random fixtures
exercise mechanics and numerical equivalence only.

The current adapter also rejects duplicate/nonfinite metadata, wrong tensor
dtypes, incomplete backbone/head state and nonfinite weights at load time.
Head tensors must be FP32; backbone storage may be FP32 or BF16. Weight scans use
bounded temporary chunks. Artifact identity hashes include consumed configs,
the optional package manifest, tokenizer and both weight files. The initial
request limit is 2,048 tokens (explicitly configurable up to the package cap);
oversized inputs are errors, not truncations. A per-segment byte ceiling of
`32 × max_length` bounds retained token-cache strings. This physical resource
limit can reject a segment that a particular tokenizer would otherwise encode
within the token cap. When a package declares a `files_sha256` table, consumed
files with declared entries must match their 64-hex digests; local bundles without
that optional table remain supported. This is integrity against the supplied
manifest, not authentication of its publisher. Exact option-token caching
is available explicitly and remains off by default until a target workload
establishes complete-request benefit.

Real BPE and FP32 MLX parity have since passed on the 77-case development assay.
Actual CUDA/BF16 parity remains unknown; the shared GPU host was occupied.

There is no evidence yet for a 20× complete-request improvement. Omitting
generation, SDPA and inference mode are already upstream baseline behavior.
Every claimed speedup must name the denominator, hardware, precision, shapes,
warm/cold policy, tokenization inclusion, latency distribution and decision/
probability drift. A head-only or repeated-menu tokenization result cannot be
reported as whole-engine acceleration. The supported first implementation is a
small, local-only adapter with exact tokens and head math; architecture,
quantization and compilation remain gated experiments; prefix sharing has no
production path.

files.text:
# CPU and CUDA inference

Kai performs one causal forward pass, then reads each candidate endpoint and the
final decision endpoint. It has no autoregressive decode loop. Wyat retains the
released segmented tokenizer recipe and FP32 decision head; replacing this with
last-token classification would change the trained contract.

PyTorch owns matrix kernels and attention dispatch. Its
[scaled dot-product attention](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html)
selects an available implementation for the device and input. Wyat defaults to
SDPA and exposes eager attention as a reference for numerical checks. Different
kernels and batch shapes can produce different floating-point rounding, so
benchmark reports retain logit differences and selected-candidate agreement.

Wyat pads only on the right and gathers only valid candidate/query endpoints.
The causal attention rule excludes every future padding position from those
readouts, so inference needs no separate padding mask or padding to a multiple
of eight. Hypothesis tests perturb future pad tokens and compare the readouts
against an independently masked reference.

CPU inference uses FP32. Thread counts belong to the process running the model,
not the reusable scorer: changing PyTorch threads affects other models in the
same process. Sweep threads on the actual machine and workload rather than
assuming more threads are faster. This follows
[PyTorch's threading guidance](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/cpu_threading_torchscript_inference.html)
and [ONNX Runtime's tuning guidance](https://onnxruntime.ai/docs/performance/tune-performance/threading.html).
Both distinguish operation parallelism from simultaneous-request parallelism.
The CLI's `--torch-threads` option sets the count at the process boundary;
omitting it preserves PyTorch's default.

CUDA inference requires a BF16-capable device. Linear parameters that were stored
as exactly representable BF16 values are restored to BF16; embeddings, norms,
the residual stream and the decision head retain FP32. Linear operations run
under BF16 autocast. Arbitrary FP32 weights are not silently rounded during
loading. CPU and CUDA therefore require explicit numerical and decision parity
checks for each released artifact.

`inference_mode` and disabled KV caching keep training graphs and unused decode
state out of the runtime. Results are materialized on the CPU before returning,
so returned scores have completed device execution. Benchmarks also synchronize
around measured CUDA work, following
[PyTorch's CUDA timing guidance](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/cuda.html#asynchronous-execution).

The architecture has similarities to
[vLLM pooling models](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/models/pooling_models/), but
Kai's candidate endpoints and shared bilinear/MLP head require a custom pooler.
Wyat does not introduce a second serving engine before that integration has a
measured benefit and passes the same artifact, tokenization and quality gates.
Compilation, weight quantization and KV prefix reuse also remain experiments
until they improve a stated real workload without unacceptable decision drift.

The real Kai release was checked on 77 fixed BANKING77 development cases with
six supplied candidates per case. Kai's exposure to the source data is unknown;
these cases check engine parity, not generalization. The simpler causal path
preserved every complete candidate ranking and selected candidate against the
previous explicit-mask path, with maximum logit difference `9.54e-7`.
Both paths classified 67 of the 77 cases correctly.
[The FP32 reference](../benchmarks/real/torch-fp32-reference77.json) retains token
IDs, endpoint positions and both sets of logits.

Seven alternating timing pairs on the fixed first 16 cases found roughly a
`1.02x` median change for causal-only attention. Singleton timing varied across
pairs, so this change supports a simpler implementation without a meaningful
CPU speedup claim. The
[singleton](../benchmarks/real/torch-causal-confirm-batch1.json) and
[batch-eight](../benchmarks/real/torch-causal-confirm-batch8.json) receipts retain
every measured output. Thread and batch choices are machine/workload settings;
the screen does not establish a portable thread default.
The [screen reproducer](../benchmarks/real/torch/causal/screen.py) and
[confirmation reproducer](../benchmarks/real/torch/causal/confirm.py) preserve
the original rounded, explicitly masked implementation as their reference.
Their default output directory keeps newly measured receipts separate from the
historical evidence.

Dynamic INT8 QNNPACK quantization was rejected. On the same 16 cases it was
approximately three times slower, changed 13 of the 16 complete rankings, and
introduced maximum logit/probability differences of `1.808`/`0.219`. It failed
the predeclared quality gate, so the 77-case follow-up was skipped and no
quantization runtime option was added. The
[reproducer](../benchmarks/real/torch/quantization.py) and
[failure-inclusive receipt](../benchmarks/real/torch-qnnpack-16.json) preserve the
experiment. This result applies to the tested QNNPACK dynamic Linear recipe on
the M4 Pro, not every quantization method or CPU.

CPU Inductor compilation was also rejected for this workload. The dedicated
subprocess completed within its 120-second budget, spending `30.62 s` on JIT
and its first 16-case cohort. Five paired warmed measurements preserved all
rankings and decisions, but compiled inference was slower in every pair:
median speedup `0.919x`, versus the unchanged FP32 engine. The
[bounded reproducer](../benchmarks/real/torch/compile.py),
[paired receipt](../benchmarks/real/torch-compile-16.json) and
[wall-time receipt](../benchmarks/real/torch-compile-wall.json) retain the result.
No compilation option was added to the runtime.

files.name: docs/training-contracts.md
files.text:
# Training and deployment boundaries

Inspected locally on 2026-10-05. These observations describe the current source
and selected artifact bytes; they do not select Wyat's final architecture or
establish deployed model quality. Training remains owned by CLM Lab and Kayak.

## Three distinct recipes

| Path | Observable contract | Deployment consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kayak public CLM | `clm-qwen3` / `clm-choice-v1`: state and candidates encoded separately, normalized last-token vectors, distinct FP32 projection heads, scaled dot products and menu softmax. Strict manifest pins encoder revision and checkpoint SHA-256. | This is an existing entrypoint pattern, not the recipe for a joint candidate-aware model. |
| Kayak joint research | Qwen3-0.6B with rank-8, alpha-16 q/v adapters; linear, MLP or shared candidate head. Segmented public candidate-line input, final query token and endpoint or mean candidate pooling. | Exact serializer, adapter configuration and pooling must accompany exported weights. Current wrapper admits only two through six candidates. |
| CLM Lab validity diagnosis | Frozen Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, separately rendered state/action or per-candidate joint text; independent binary-validity logits. | These logits are not a mutually exclusive Choice distribution. Applying menu softmax changes their meaning. The primary model failed its declared quality gate. |

Kayak's public artifact contract is documented in
`/Users/teilomillet/Code/kayak/docs/model-contract.md` and implemented by
`kayak/bundle.py`, `kayak/runtime/_loading.py` and `kayak/runtime/_model.py`.
Its manifest includes family, input recipe, pinned encoder identity, width,
context limit, checkpoint filename and integrity hash. It refuses remote Python
code and unrestricted checkpoint pickle loading. Later recipes need their own
implementation and independent reference fixtures.

## Joint candidate-aware research, exactly as inspected

The source owner is
`/Users/teilomillet/Code/kayak/benchmarks/decision_search/model.py`, with backbone
and adapter ownership in `benchmarks/prerequisites/model.py`.

- Backbone: `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` revision
  `c1899de289a04d12100db370d81485cdf75e47ca`, hidden width 1,024.
- Prompt recipe: `public-candidate-lines-segmented-no-special-tokens-v1`.
  Prefix, each complete `A. description` line, newline separators and suffix
  are tokenized separately with no special tokens and no truncation. Concatenated
  segments reproduce every original character. The default cap is 1,536 tokens.
- Candidates: two through six unique contiguous lines labeled A–F in display
  order. Descriptions are single-line; suffix is exactly `\n\nDecision:` or
  `\nReturn only the letter of the next action.`. Other renderings fail.
- Query: final non-padding token under contiguous right padding.
- Candidate readout: LayerNorms, bias-free key/query projections to 256,
  bilinear dot product divided by square-root 256, plus a shared GELU scalar
  branch. Candidate pooling is an explicit `endpoint` or `mean` setting.
- Weights: only q/v adapter matrices and the selected head are saved in
  Safetensors. Restore checks exact tensor names, shape, dtype and finiteness.
  Backbone weights, tokenizer and deployment recipe are not embedded.

The shared head accepts an arbitrary number of already-computed candidate
vectors algebraically. The current serializer, batch spans, training masks and
measurement contract enforce six slots. Larger menus need a versioned input
and result contract plus training/evaluation evidence. A displayed candidate
with unmet prerequisites must remain scored; only padding is masked.

Candidate vectors depend on the complete preceding causal prompt. They cannot
be cached by candidate text alone. Permuting fixed feature vectors permutes
shared-head scores, but permuting prompt lines changes the feature vectors.
End-to-end order invariance is therefore unestablished.

One concrete available checkpoint is
`/Users/teilomillet/Code/kayak/.benchmarks/joint-search-20261003/runtime-quality-v1/seed43_final_repeat_fast/last.safetensors`.
Its directly verified SHA-256 is
`1df83f58cad070efe4adebcfee691ae2897b6f099172e91848ac5fd75c30a10e`.
The header has 112 adapter tensors, `head.weight [6,1024]`, `head.bias [6]` and
no metadata: this is a **linear-slot** artifact. No candidate-head checkpoint
was found among Safetensors files under that research directory in this
inspection. Candidate-head source availability is not a deployable model.

## CLM Lab's retained diagnostic artifact

The primary checkpoint exists at
`/Users/teilomillet/Code/clm-lab/runs/wyat-validity-diagnosis-20261003/training/joint-validity-n2048-s17/step-0512.pt`.
Its directly verified SHA-256 is
`d0b2be9c6bf884b7635555d9a4dfc3ae0685660ebfe98fc522f9685e09a4b68d`.
The retained report records 53.94% novel balanced accuracy and zero of 512
complete novel groups; no checkpoint was promoted. This assay is development
evidence, not an official Wyat or Decision Index score.

The frozen adapter in `lab/tools/wyat_diagnosis/infer.py` binds model spec,
encoder recipe and source hashes. Inputs contain only `id`, `state`, `question`
and candidates `{id,text}`. Rendering is:

```text
state:  Instruct: {question}\nQuery: {state}
action: {candidate_text}
joint:  Instruct: {question}\nQuery: {state}\nDocument: {candidate_text}
```

Candidate IDs and other menu entries are not rendered into the joint pair.
The adapter returns independent logits, with zero as its assay threshold;
sigmoid values are uncalibrated outside that assay. Its archived loader uses
`torch.load(weights_only=False)`, acceptable only within its sealed experiment
trust boundary. Wyat should not expose that path as a general user-model loader.
Exporting tensor-only weights with a strict manifest is the necessary boundary
before admitting this format, even for diagnostic replay.

## Export requirements before admitting another recipe

Keep user-facing requests independent of head architecture, but make each
supported backend's obligations explicit. A deployable export must bind:

1. Format version, model family, input recipe and exact artifact identity.
2. Backbone/tokenizer revisions or verified local files; weight hashes and
   tensor-only head/adapters; exact expected names, shapes and dtypes.
3. Rendering/tokenization, padding, cap and overflow behavior; candidate
   identity/order/span rules; pooling, normalization and adapter parameters.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any, Dict, Optional, Union

import mlx.core as mx
import mlx.nn as nn
from mlx.nn.layers.distributed import shard_linear

from .activations import swiglu
from .base import BaseModelArgs, create_attention_mask, scaled_dot_product_attention
from .rope_utils import initialize_rope


@dataclass
class ModelArgs(BaseModelArgs):
    model_type: str
    hidden_size: int
    num_hidden_layers: int
    intermediate_size: int
    num_attention_heads: int
    rms_norm_eps: float
    vocab_size: int
    num_key_value_heads: int
    max_position_embeddings: int = 32768
    rope_theta: float = 1000000
    rope_traditional: bool = False
    rope_scaling: Optional[Dict[str, Union[float, str]]] = None
    tie_word_embeddings: bool = True


class Attention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, args: ModelArgs):
        super().__init__()

        dim = args.hidden_size
        self.n_heads = n_heads = args.num_attention_heads
        assert args.num_key_value_heads is not None
        self.n_kv_heads = n_kv_heads = args.num_key_value_heads

        head_dim = args.hidden_size // n_heads
        self.scale = head_dim**-0.5

        self.q_proj = nn.Linear(dim, n_heads * head_dim, bias=True)
        self.k_proj = nn.Linear(dim, n_kv_heads * head_dim, bias=True)
        self.v_proj = nn.Linear(dim, n_kv_heads * head_dim, bias=True)
        self.o_proj = nn.Linear(n_heads * head_dim, dim, bias=False)

        self.rope = initialize_rope(
            head_dim,
            base=args.rope_theta,
            traditional=args.rope_traditional,
            scaling_config=args.rope_scaling,
            max_position_embeddings=args.max_position_embeddings,
        )

    def __call__(
        self,
        x: mx.array,
        mask: Optional[mx.array] = None,
        cache: Optional[Any] = None,
    ) -> mx.array:
        B, L, D = x.shape

        queries, keys, values = self.q_proj(x), self.k_proj(x), self.v_proj(x)

        # Prepare the queries, keys and values for the attention computation
        queries = queries.reshape(B, L, self.n_heads, -1).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)
        keys = keys.reshape(B, L, self.n_kv_heads, -1).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)
        values = values.reshape(B, L, self.n_kv_heads, -1).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)

        if cache is not None:
            queries = self.rope(queries, offset=cache.offset)
            keys = self.rope(keys, offset=cache.offset)
            keys, values = cache.update_and_fetch(keys, values)
        else:
            queries = self.rope(queries)
            keys = self.rope(keys)

        output = scaled_dot_product_attention(
            queries, keys, values, cache=cache, scale=self.scale, mask=mask
        )
        output = output.transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(B, L, -1)
        return self.o_proj(output)


class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim, hidden_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.gate_proj = nn.Linear(dim, hidden_dim, bias=False)
        self.down_proj = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, dim, bias=False)
        self.up_proj = nn.Linear(dim, hidden_dim, bias=False)

    def __call__(self, x) -> mx.array:
        return self.down_proj(swiglu(self.gate_proj(x), self.up_proj(x)))


class TransformerBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, args: ModelArgs):
        super().__init__()
        self.num_attention_heads = args.num_attention_heads
        self.hidden_size = args.hidden_size
        self.self_attn = Attention(args)
        self.mlp = MLP(args.hidden_size, args.intermediate_size)
        self.input_layernorm = nn.RMSNorm(args.hidden_size, eps=args.rms_norm_eps)
        self.post_attention_layernorm = nn.RMSNorm(
            args.hidden_size, eps=args.rms_norm_eps
        )
        self.args = args

    def __call__(
        self,
        x: mx.array,
        mask: Optional[mx.array] = None,
        cache: Optional[Any] = None,
    ) -> mx.array:
        r = self.self_attn(self.input_layernorm(x), mask, cache)
        h = x + r
        r = self.mlp(self.post_attention_layernorm(h))
        out = h + r
        return out


class Qwen2Model(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, args: ModelArgs):
        super().__init__()
        self.args = args
        self.vocab_size = args.vocab_size
        self.num_hidden_layers = args.num_hidden_layers
        assert self.vocab_size > 0
        self.embed_tokens = nn.Embedding(args.vocab_size, args.hidden_size)
        self.layers = [
            TransformerBlock(args=args) for _ in range(args.num_hidden_layers)
        ]
        self.norm = nn.RMSNorm(args.hidden_size, eps=args.rms_norm_eps)

    def __call__(
        self,
        inputs: mx.array,
        cache=None,
        input_embeddings: Optional[mx.array] = None,
    ):
        if input_embeddings is not None:
            h = input_embeddings
        else:
            h = self.embed_tokens(inputs)

        if cache is None:
            cache = [None] * len(self.layers)
        mask = create_attention_mask(h, cache[0])

        for layer, c in zip(self.layers, cache):
            h = layer(h, mask, c)

        return self.norm(h)


class Model(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, args: ModelArgs):
        super().__init__()
        self.args = args
        self.model_type = args.model_type
        self.model = Qwen2Model(args)
        if not args.tie_word_embeddings:
            self.lm_head = nn.Linear(args.hidden_size, args.vocab_size, bias=False)

    def __call__(
        self,
        inputs: mx.array,
        cache=None,
        input_embeddings: Optional[mx.array] = None,
    ):
        out = self.model(inputs, cache, input_embeddings)
        if self.args.tie_word_embeddings:
            out = self.model.embed_tokens.as_linear(out)
        else:
            out = self.lm_head(out)
        return out

    def sanitize(self, weights):
        if self.args.tie_word_embeddings:
            weights.pop("lm_head.weight", None)
        # Remove unused precomputed rotary freqs
        return {
            k: v for k, v in weights.items() if "self_attn.rotary_emb.inv_freq" not in k
        }

    def shard(self, group: Optional[mx.distributed.Group] = None):
        group = group or mx.distributed.init()
        N = group.size()
        for layer in self.model.layers:
            # Shard the self attention
            layer.self_attn.q_proj = shard_linear(
                layer.self_attn.q_proj, "all-to-sharded", group=group
            )
            layer.self_attn.k_proj = shard_linear(
                layer.self_attn.k_proj, "all-to-sharded", group=group
            )
            layer.self_attn.v_proj = shard_linear(
                layer.self_attn.v_proj, "all-to-sharded", group=group
            )
            layer.self_attn.o_proj = shard_linear(
                layer.self_attn.o_proj, "sharded-to-all", group=group
            )
            layer.self_attn.n_heads //= N
            layer.self_attn.n_kv_heads //= N

            # Shard the MLP
            layer.mlp.gate_proj = shard_linear(
                layer.mlp.gate_proj, "all-to-sharded", group=group
            )
            layer.mlp.down_proj = shard_linear(
                layer.mlp.down_proj, "sharded-to-all", group=group
            )
            layer.mlp.up_proj = shard_linear(
                layer.mlp.up_proj, "all-to-sharded", group=group
            )

    @property
    def layers(self):
        return self.model.layers

def fractional_max_pool2d_with_indices(
    input: Tensor,
    kernel_size: BroadcastingList2[int],
    output_size: Optional[BroadcastingList2[int]] = None,  # noqa: UP045
    output_ratio: Optional[BroadcastingList2[float]] = None,  # noqa: UP045
    return_indices: bool = False,
    _random_samples: Tensor | None = None,
) -> tuple[Tensor, Tensor]:
    r"""
    fractional_max_pool2d(input, kernel_size, output_size=None, output_ratio=None, return_indices=False, _random_samples=None)

    Applies 2D fractional max pooling over an input signal composed of several input planes.

    Fractional MaxPooling is described in detail in the paper `Fractional MaxPooling`_ by Ben Graham

    The max-pooling operation is applied in :math:`kH \times kW` regions by a stochastic
    step size determined by the target output size.
    The number of output features is equal to the number of input planes.

    Args:
        kernel_size: the size of the window to take a max over.
                     Can be a single number :math:`k` (for a square kernel of :math:`k \times k`)
                     or a tuple `(kH, kW)`
        output_size: the target output size of the image of the form :math:`oH \times oW`.
                     Can be a tuple `(oH, oW)` or a single number :math:`oH` for a square image :math:`oH \times oH`
        output_ratio: If one wants to have an output size as a ratio of the input size, this option can be given.
                      This has to be a number or tuple in the range (0, 1)
        return_indices: if ``True``, will return the indices along with the outputs.
                        Useful to pass to :func:`~torch.nn.functional.max_unpool2d`.

    Examples::
        >>> input = torch.randn(20, 16, 50, 32)
        >>> # pool of square window of size=3, and target output size 13x12
        >>> F.fractional_max_pool2d(input, 3, output_size=(13, 12))
        >>> # pool of square window and target output size being half of input image size
        >>> F.fractional_max_pool2d(input, 3, output_ratio=(0.5, 0.5))

    .. _Fractional MaxPooling:
        http://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6071
    """
    if has_torch_function_variadic(input, _random_samples):
        return handle_torch_function(
            fractional_max_pool2d_with_indices,
            (input, _random_samples),
            input,
            kernel_size,
            output_size=output_size,
            output_ratio=output_ratio,
            return_indices=return_indices,
            _random_samples=_random_samples,
        )
    if output_size is None and output_ratio is None:
        raise ValueError(
            "fractional_max_pool2d requires specifying either an output_size or an output_ratio"
        )
    if output_size is None:
        if output_ratio is None:
            raise AssertionError("output_ratio is unexpectedly None")
        if len(output_ratio) > 2:
            raise ValueError(
                "fractional_max_pool2d requires output_ratio to either be a single Int or tuple of Ints."
            )
        _output_ratio = _pair(output_ratio)
        output_size = [
            int(input.size(-2) * _output_ratio[0]),
            int(input.size(-1) * _output_ratio[1]),
        ]

    if _random_samples is None:
        n_batch = 1 if input.dim() == 3 else input.size(0)
        _random_samples = torch.rand(
            n_batch, input.size(-3), 2, dtype=input.dtype, device=input.device
        )
    return torch._C._nn.fractional_max_pool2d(
        input, kernel_size, output_size, _random_samples
    )
